items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Wildlife 2027 Calendars Supporting Conservation Turn Everyday Walls into Year-Round Fundraising Reading Time: 3 minutes From orphaned elephants in Kenya to red fox kits in Virginia, this year’s wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation prove that a simple wall calendar can still fund real protection work. Wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation span continents and causes this year, each turning monthly wall space into sustained fundraising for the species and landscapes they feature. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s 2027 Calendar brings twelve images from the Orphans’ Project in Kenya, following rescued elephants and other wildlife raised at the trust’s facilities, with every purchase directed toward rescue, protection, and conservation work across the country. The double-page format includes a centrefold poster alongside UK, Kenya, Canada, and USA holidays, pairing each enchanting monthly scene with insight into the orphaned animals’ individual journeys. In South Africa, Crow KZN Wildlife Calendars continue a long-running tradition supporting the Centre for Rehabilitation of Wildlife in KwaZulu-Natal, channeling calendar sales directly into the rescue and rehabilitation of injured, orphaned, and displaced wild animals across the region. These wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation represent some of the most grassroots fundraising efforts on this list, tying purchases to a single rehabilitation center’s daily operating costs. WWF’s 2027 Wildlife Calendars , available through major retail calendar outlets, extend the organization’s global conservation brand into one of its most accessible fundraising products. Featuring iconic endangered species synonymous with WWF’s decades of conservation advocacy, these calendars let supporters bring the organization’s mission into homes and offices while contributing to broader habitat protection and anti-poaching initiatives worldwide. State wildlife agencies produce some of the most enduring entries among wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation. Virginia’s Department of Wildlife Resources marks a milestone with its 2027 edition, celebrating 50 years of the iconic Virginia Wildlife calendar. This anniversary edition features photographs dedicated to juvenile wildlife, refreshed wildlife facts, with a red fox kit by photographer Anne Bryant gracing the cover. Calendar sales support the department’s ongoing wildlife management and conservation programs across the state. The Alaska Wildlife Alliance takes a distinctly participatory approach to wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation. Rather than commissioning professional photography, the organization invites photographers worldwide to submit images through an annual contest, with thirteen winning photographs selected to fill the 2027 Alaska Wildlife Calendar. Winning photographers donate their images and receive complimentary copies in exchange, while all calendar sale proceeds fund the alliance’s work protecting Alaska’s wildlife and wild places. The model doubles as community engagement, turning calendar production itself into a celebration shared between contributing photographers and the conservation mission their images support. Not every wildlife calendar funds a conservation organization directly, but many still advance public appreciation for biodiversity that underpins broader protection efforts. Wildlife photographer Max Waugh’s 2027 collection includes nine themed calendars, five featuring new images and four returning favorites. This year’s new themes include Yellowstone wildlife and scenery, a twelve-species Wild Cats collection photographed in the wild worldwide, a Top Birds collection, a first-ever Borneo calendar highlighting Malaysian wildlife including proboscis monkeys, and a crowdsourced Odd Couples theme capturing interspecies interactions. Returning Classic calendars cover Brazil’s Pantanal and Amazon wildlife, African elephants in black and white, broader animal landscapes, and hornbills and toucans across Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Wildlife photographer Max Waugh’s 2027 Top Birds calendar showcases his favorite wild birds photographed worldwide, one of nine themed calendars he released this year, spanning Yellowstone wildlife, big cats, Borneo species, and more, and advancing public appreciation for biodiversity even without direct conservation funding. Photo courtesy of Max Waugh . What unites wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation across such different organizations and formats is a shared bet that sustained, monthly visual contact with wildlife translates into sustained public support for protecting it. A calendar hanging in a kitchen or office does more than mark dates. Each month’s image becomes a recurring reminder of orphaned elephants recovering in Kenya, native species submitted by state artists, or rehabilitation centers operating on tight budgets in South Africa. This funding model carries genuine significance for smaller organizations in particular. Rehabilitation centers and state wildlife diversity programs often operate without the large donor bases that fund major international conservation groups, making modest, recurring purchases like calendar sales a meaningful and predictable revenue stream. For buyers, the appeal combines practical utility with values-aligned spending, offering a tangible, daily-use product supporting causes they care about without requiring a separate donation decision each time. As 2027 approaches, these calendars demonstrate that even simple products can carry outsized conservation impact when organizations consistently invest in quality photography , compelling storytelling, and transparent connections between purchase and purpose. Whether featuring an orphaned elephant finding its feet in Kenya or a red fox kit marking a state program’s fiftieth anniversary, wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation prove that protecting wildlife can start with something as ordinary as checking today’s date. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through a forest in the Eastern Himalayas after sunset. The ground is damp, fallen leaves gather beneath towering trees, and the sounds of insects fill the night air. Somewhere among the undergrowth, a tiny frog sits almost unnoticed, blending into its surroundings. In forests like these, some of nature's most fascinating discoveries are easy to miss. And a recent scientific study has brought five such hidden inhabitants into the spotlight. Researchers from the University of Delhi and Harvard University have identified five previously unknown species of horned frogs in Arunachal Pradesh, following five years of fieldwork in the Eastern Himalayas. The discovery has also revealed something unusual about one of them: it feeds on land snails, making it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India. The research offers a fascinating glimpse into the biodiversity that India's forests continue to hold. Meet the five newly discovered frogs All five species belong to the genus Jingophrys , commonly known as diminutive horned frogs. These tiny to medium-sized amphibians are distinguished by horn-like projections of skin around their eyes, which give them their distinctive appearance. The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii) is named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, incorporating the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Photograph: ( The Times of India ) The five newly identified species are: Tanii horned frog ( Jingophrys taniitatii ): Named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, the name also incorporates 'tatii', the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Snail-eating horned frog ( Jingophrys tanogogo ): Named after the Apatani word for snails, this species has an especially unusual diet. Siang horned frog ( Jingophrys siangensis ): Named after the Siang region of Arunachal Pradesh, where it was discovered. Hrdy's horned frog ( Jingophrys hrdy ): Named in recognition of a long-time supporter of herpetological research and conservation biology at Harvard University. Wu-Larson's horned frog ( Jingophrys wularsoni ): Also named to recognise supporters of research and conservation at Harvard. The names of three species acknowledge the region's local communities, language and geography, while the other two honour individuals who have supported scientific research. A frog that eats snails, shells and all! Among the five discoveries, Jingophrys tanogogo stands out for its unusual feeding behaviour. While examining the species, researchers used advanced three-dimensional micro-CT imaging to study its internal anatomy. They found entire land snail shells inside the frog's gut. The snail-eating horned frog (Jingophrys tanogogo) is India's first recorded frog species known to consume land snails, shells and all. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) This makes it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India and the first documented instance of snail-eating behaviour in the family Megophryidae. It is a remarkable finding because it expands what scientists know about the feeding habits of this group of amphibians. Five years of research in challenging terrain Identifying these frogs was no easy task. The research team included Sonali Garg, S D Biju, Tage Tajo, Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K, and James Hanken, who carried out extensive explorations across the Eastern Himalayas. The researchers encountered temperatures as low as minus 4 degrees Celsius while navigating the mountainous terrain. Since these frogs are nocturnal, much of the fieldwork involved searching for them at night, often without a place to stay. Researchers used advanced 3D micro-CT imaging to examine the frogs' anatomy, discovering entire land snail shells inside one species' gut. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) Local tribal communities also played an important role, sharing their knowledge of the region and supporting the researchers during their field explorations. Beyond identifying new species, the team used DNA analysis to understand their evolutionary history. Their findings suggest that the diversification of these frogs coincided with the rise of the Himalayan mountain ranges and the intensification of the Asian monsoon millions of years ago. Why these discoveries matter The findings draw attention to the Eastern Himalayas as an important centre of biodiversity and evolution. The number of Jingophrys species recorded in India has increased seven-fold through this research, while the known diversity of the genus worldwide has more than doubled. Yet, there is still much to learn. Some of these frogs are extremely secretive and appear in remote forests only during short breeding seasons. Further research will be needed to understand their ecology, behaviour and conservation needs. The five-year research involved night-time explorations across the challenging terrain of the Eastern Himalayas, with local tribal communities helping researchers navigate the region. Photograph: ( Indian Expresss ) For now, these five discoveries offer a reminder of how much life remains undocumented in India's forests. Sometimes, finding an entirely new species does not require looking beyond a distant wilderness. It simply requires looking a little closer at the world beneath our feet. Sources: 'New frog species found in Arunachal, Keralam scientist part of team' by K S Sreejith for The New Indian Express, Published on 14 November 2026. 'Two-fold hidden diversity of diminutive horned frogs (Megophryinae: Jingophrys) highlights overlooked in situ diversification in the Himalayas' by PUBMED.

Το alter ego του χαρακτήρα Peanuts είναι μέρος της 100ης απόδοσης της παρέλασης, η οποία αρχικά ήταν προγραμματισμένη να πραγματοποιηθεί σήμερα, αλλά έχει προγραμματιστεί εκ νέου για το πρωί του Σαββάτου λόγω των έντονων καιρικών συνθηκών…
items.descriptionOriginal: Snoopy — or should we say Joe Cool — will be celebrating something big when he floats through New York City during the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The Peanuts character’s alter ego is part of the 100th rendition of the parade, which was originally slated to take place today but has been rescheduled to Saturday morning due to severe weather. “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said Wednesday, per NBC News . “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers, and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” The event began in 1924 and has run annually ever since, except for three years during World War II. Each November, the retail company adds new balloons to its lineup of massive inflatables, a signature feature of the parade almost from the beginning. The first, introduced in 1927, was Felix the Cat, a hit cartoon character from the silent film era . It was designed by Tony Sarg, a puppeteer and illustrator credited with helping turn the parade into the spectacle it is today. George Rinhart—Corbis Historical/Getty Images Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, November 24, 1932. Unlike today, however, the inaugural balloon had to be carried on stilts , as helium wouldn’t be used until the following year. Other aspects also evolved considerably in the ensuing decades, including the long process of bringing a balloon from sketch to showpiece. Artists kick it off with simple drawings, which are then digitally rendered and approved by engineers. Next, a small model is 3D-printed — a physical pattern for the full-scale version that’s made of fabric coated in polyurethane. “[The model] enables us to map out exactly where all of our cuts and all of our seams are going to be,” Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy’s Studios, told Today during a tour of the studio where the balloons are constructed, adding: “Similar to creating a garment for clothing, all of those pieces are the 3D model flattened out.” The final steps are heat-sealing the pieces together, hand-painting the balloon, and adding about 12,000 cubic feet of helium. Just over a century following Felix’s debut, he’s back for this year’s festivities — a decade after his last appearance. He’s joining dozens of other inflatables for a record-breaking 100 in total. Take a look at the nine new balloons created for the centennial celebration. items.title: Οι Portlanders μετατρέπουν το διασωθέν φαγητό σε ποιοτικά γεύματα εστιατορίου
items.titleOriginal: The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals
items.description: Είμαι Τρίτη πρωί στις αρχές Οκτωβρίου και ο σεφ Bradley Cohen, 49 ετών, προσπαθεί να αυτοσχεδιάσει ένα γεύμα από ένα τηγάνι ξενοδοχείου γεμάτο με χοιρινά φιλέτα. Βγάζει ένα κλουβί με φρέσκο ​​λάχανο και κολοκυθάκια από το δωμάτιο, σημειώνοντας την ημερομηνία που έφερε (Κυριακή) και λέει ότι πιθανότατα θα ζεματίσει τα λαχανικά. «Το πρόβλημα δεν είναι ότι δεν υπάρχει αρκετό φαγητό - είναι απλώς μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: I t’s a Tuesday morning in early October and chef Bradley Cohen, 49, is trying to improvise a meal from a hotel pan full of pork loins. He pulls a crate of fresh kale and zucchini from the walk-in, noting the date it was brought in (Sunday), and says he’ll probably blanch the veggies. “The problem is not that there’s not enough food — it’s just in the wrong places,” he says. Bradley Cohen is among the chefs who turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals for Urban Gleaners. Credit: Hannah Wallace He checks out the spices and other ingredients that have appeared in the pantry since his last visit to this centrally located kitchen and grows animated when he finds a container of gochujang, a savory-spicy fermented condiment popular in Korean cooking. “I always get excited when I find this because it adds umami,” he says. He decides on the spot that he’ll make a gochujang-veggie bouillon braising sauce for the pork loins. To complete the meal, he’ll make some macaroni, tossed in butter, garlic powder and paprika. This madcap cooking challenge isn’t for Chopped . It’s for a Portland, Oregon-based gleaning organization. Urban Gleaners is a 20-year-old nonprofit that rescues food before it goes into the waste stream — and helps feed hungry Portlanders. Gleaning, the practice of collecting leftover crops from farmers’ fields or orchards, is nothing new: There are references to gleaning in the Bible, and it was widely employed by the rural poor in the 16th and 17th centuries. And today, there are hundreds of gleaning nonprofits across the U.S. But Urban Gleaners’ cooking program is unique. Helmed by chef Jason Howd, a former pastry chef and caterer who has bee n with the organization for nine years, the cooking program allows part-time chefs like Cohen, a former marketing director, to turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals. The braised pork, pasta and kale (he ends up sautéing it and tossing in some tomatillo salsa for acid) that Cohen makes today will be refrigerated overnight and packed up the next morning by volunteers, then hand-delivered to shopping-style pantries at local parks, schools and community centers. Perhaps surprisingly, these ingredients aren’t past their sell-by dates. The kale, in particular, looks fresh from the garden. Turns out it was picked two days ago from a nearby farm that sells at the King Farmers Market in Northeast Portland. (Many farms would rather donate surplus fresh organic produce than transport it back to the farm, where they often don’t have storage space.) The pork loins were purchased at a local chef’s supply store. (Donated protein can be hard to come by, so Urban Gleaners has a budget to purchase pork, chicken and other meats.) Delicious prepared meals are just one service Urban Gleaners provides. Haris Kuljančić, the organization’s new executive director, says the need for food has never been greater. The nonprofit delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations — including elementary schools, community centers and housing complexes. “We turn it around really quickly,” he says. On this day alone, a Tuesday, the organization will deliver 2,000 pounds of food — mostly gleaned items and prepared food from nearby grocery stores like New Seasons and Zupan’s Market as well as Elephant’s Delicatessen — to a “park market” at Mount Scott Community Center. Urban Gleaners runs three such markets that are open to the public. Urban Gleaners delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations. Credit: Hannah Wallace In July 2025, President Trump’s H.R. 1 (aka “the Big Beautiful Bill”) cut SNAP funding — i.e. food stamps — by $186 billion. Tighter eligibility restrictions — such as an 80-hour-a-month work requirement for those under 65 and eliminated benefits for refugees, asylum seekers and houseless folks — have resulted in SNAP participation falling by around 13 percent nationwide , according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ SNAP tracker. There are a handful of exemptions (if you’re pregnant, have a child under 14 living with you, or are enrolled in a school or training program, for example) but many SNAP recipients don’t know about these. Another change: H.R. 1 requires that folks reapply for benefits every six months. “They are forcing people to go through the eligibility again, and so if they don’t re-enroll, or don’t jump through all the hoops, you risk losing benefits,” explains Stephanie Barr, executive director of Lift Urban Portland ( Lift UP), a gleaning nonprofit that focuses on feeding neighbors in downtown and Northwest Portland. Needless to say, this can be a challenge for houseless folks (who typically don’t have mailing addresses) and seniors (for whom filling out paperwork can be a burden). In Oregon, these cuts and new restrictions have meant that more than 94,000 Oregonians lost SNAP benefits over the past year, according to the latest data from the Oregon Department of Human Services. This, of course, has led to increased demand at food pantries and the gleaning markets run by Urban Gleaners and others. It’s impossible to fill the void entirely with gleaned food, but Portland area gleaning nonprofits sure are trying. “We hear a lot from the folks we serve about the impacts of SNAP cuts. And the cost of increased food prices,” says Barr, who notes that many of the seniors Lift UP serves are on a fixed income. “Even if you live in affordable housing, your rent can go up. That’s happening in our community.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Lift UP has a shopping-style food pantry in southwest Portland that serves 17,000 people annually. It also delivers food boxes to 550 residents across 50 low-income housing complexes through its “ Adopt a Building ” program. (Lift UP also sponsors pop-up farmers markets in half of those buildings, so residents can access fresh fruits and vegetables.) Like Urban Gleaners, Lift UP mostly gets donations from grocery stores as well as the Oregon Food Bank, community food drives and bakeries such as Grand Central, which makes a “community loaf” especially for anti-hunger organizations. Still, even with all these gleaned groceries, Barr says that over a third of the people that Lift UP serves via Adopt a Building have had to choose between paying rent and buying food. In September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. Credit: Leesa Morales In 2024, partly in response to cuts to the USDA’s Local Food Purchasing Assistance grants as well as rising grocery costs, Barr and leaders of other Portland-based gleaning and nutrition organizations came together to form a collective called the Coalition to Advance Food Equity (CAFE). “We really need labor, infrastructure and transportation to maximize the gleaned food,” Barr says. The goal of CAFE is to create a more resilient local food system by maximizing bulk purchasing. Eventually the hope is that CAFE will operate a larger physical food hub that all 14 member organizations can use. (Currently, Lift UP’s warehouse works as a de facto food hub. The nonprofit often takes more food than it can use, so the rest is shared with CAFE partners.) So far, CAFE has done a bulk food purchasing pilot project with Costco as well as with local businesses like Bob’s Red Mill. In October, CAFE also launched a “Farm to Food Assistance” pilot with two local regenerative farms, moving 1,000 pounds of organic produce from Stoneboat Farm and CAMPO (Colaboración Agrícola Mobilizando Poder Orgánico) to partner pantries. This is a mutually beneficial investment: Local farms get much-needed income, and the communities that CAFE members feed get high-quality produce. At Urban Gleaners’ summer fundraiser, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. Credit: Leesa Morales Another CAFE member is the Portland Fruit Tree Project (PFTP), a 20-year-old organization that dispatches volunteers around town to pick fruit from Portlanders’ yards — apples, figs, Asian pears, grapes and more. The harvest is then distributed to food pantries, homeless service organizations and other nonprofits. For its Summer Supper fundraiser, Urban Gleaners asked 15 Portland-area chefs to create dishes from mostly gleaned items. Credit: Leesa Morales Excess fruit gets made into jam, syrup or other products to extend its shelf life. Food preserver is the most popular volunteer position at PFTP. “These volunteers come in and look at what we’ve got, and we kind of decide: Are we going to can it? Are we going to dehydrate it? Are we going to juice it and use it later? Are we just going to prep it for the freezer because we’ve got too much to do right now?” says Executive Director Heather Keisler Fornes. “Yesterday we were making plum syrup that’s delicious and it’s bright pink — so pretty.” Kousa dogwood refrigerator jelly and sea buckthorn jelly were two of the more unusual items volunteers recently made. Some of these are sold at farmers’ markets and craft fairs — which helps spread the word about the Portland Fruit Tree Project. Being part of CAFE has many benefits, says Keisler Fornes. “There are times where one group has too much of something, and it’s so easy to be able to then communicate with the entire group and say, ‘Who wants this?’ Then it’s not a burden to anybody,” she says. The different CAFE members even share staff. Busy season for PFTP is summer and fall. After that, some of Keisler Fornes’s staff work for Lift UP or other nonprofits in the CAFE coalition. I n September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. They asked 15 Portland-area chefs to accede to a unique challenge: Create a dish out of mostly gleaned items. The inventiveness and talent on display was remarkable. Mika Paredes, chef at French-inspired bistro L’Echelle, made a ratatouille tartine with basil and whipped brie. Ryan Roadhouse, who had just won a James Beard Award for his Japanese omakase menus at Nodoguro, created curried Oregon bay shrimp with cherry tomatoes and spiced seaweed. And Jacob Smutko, one of the chefs at Javelina, a unique restaurant focused on the foods of the Indigenous tribes of the Pacific Northwest, made sumac and corn ribs with sikil pak (a traditional Mayan pepita dip made with cherry tomatoes, poblano peppers, onions, lime and cilantro). Emphasizing Urban Gleaners’ mission to fight food waste, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. It was a uniquely Portland experience — celebrating the city’s vibrant food scene while also highlighting the power of upcycled ingredients and supporting an organization that fights food waste and food insecurity at the same time. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime “No one should have to worry where their next meal is coming from, especially when there’s so much perfectly good food available,” says Gregory Gourdet, chef at Haitian restaurant Kann and an Urban Gleaners board member. “I love that Urban Gleaners puts feeding people at the center of its mission while also addressing food waste. It’s not just about rescuing food; it’s about feeding our neighbors, supporting families, and making sure people in our community don’t go hungry.” The post The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Η Προστασία της Φύσης μετέφερε τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: More than 400 years after colonists took corn, disturbed graves, and exchanged gunfire with Nauset warriors near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, 126 acres of salt marsh and ancestral habitat have been returned to Indigenous stewardship -- land that overlooks the very beach where that first hostile encounter took place. The Nature Conservancy transferred the property to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit founded by Ramona Peters of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, who sees the moment as an opening rather than a closing: "This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed." The land has been joined to an adjacent parcel now named T8nup hs Uwatuhsh t -- "at the turtle's nest" in the W pan ak language -- where tribal families are invited to forage, fish, hold ceremony, and belong again to a place their ancestors tended for more than 12,000 years. What the transfer quietly insists upon is that history is not only something to be corrected in textbooks; sometimes it can be corrected in deeds. "Returning this land to Indigenous ownership is historical and an act of resilience after four centuries of dispossession," Peters said -- and in that resilience, something older than the wound is still alive.

items.description: Ήταν ο πατέρας που έπαιζε καρόμ με τις κόρες του, άκουγε τις ιστορίες τους στο κολέγιο και ποτέ δεν έφερε το άγχος της δουλειάς στο σπίτι. Αλλά στις 27 Νοεμβρίου 2008, ο Tukaram Omble δεν επέστρεψε ποτέ στο σπίτι. Πρώην στρατιώτης του Ινδικού Στρατού και Βοηθός Υπο-Επιθεωρητή στην Αστυνομία της Βομβάης, ο Όμπλ ήταν σε υπηρεσία κατά τη διάρκεια των τραγικών γεγονότων της 26/11 στη Βομβάη. Εμφάνιση extrao…
items.descriptionOriginal: He was the father who played carrom with his daughters, listened to their college stories and never brought the stress of work home. But on 27 November 2008, Tukaram Omble never returned home. A former Indian Army soldier and Assistant Sub-Inspector with Mumbai Police, Omble was on duty during the tragic events of 26/11 in Mumbai. Displaying extraordinary courage and selflessness, the 54-year-old put his duty above his own life. His bravery played a crucial role in helping Mumbai Police bring a key accused into custody. For his exceptional service and supreme sacrifice, Omble was posthumously awarded the Ashoka Chakra. But for his four daughters, he was much more than a decorated officer. He was their closest companion, their go-to person and the father who always reassured them that everything would be alright. That night, he told his daughter Vaishali not to worry about him. He had always kept his work worries away from home. Even in his final hours, he was trying to protect his family from them. India remembers his courage. His daughters remember the man who made home feel safe. #TukaramOmble #2611MumbaiAttacks #MumbaiPolice #AshokaChakra [Tukaram Omble, Tukaram Omble story, 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks, 26/11 heroes, Mumbai Police heroes, Ashoka Chakra awardee]

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News EU Greenwashing Ban for Businesses Puts Proof Behind Green Claims Reading Time: 3 minutes The EU greenwashing ban for businesses is now in effect, giving shoppers clearer and more trustworthy environmental information. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses began applying on September 27, 2026. The European Union (EU) adopted it through the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive . Shoppers now get clearer and more honest environmental information. Greenwashing means making a product sound more eco-friendly than it really is. Under the new rules, vague claims must be backed up with evidence. Terms like “green,” “sustainable,” and “energy efficient” now require excellent environmental performance. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses also targets carbon offset claims. Offsetting means funding projects elsewhere to balance out a company’s emissions. Claims of a neutral, reduced, or positive impact, such as carbon neutral or net zero, cannot rely on offsets. Broad claims face limits too. A company cannot describe an entire product as eco-friendly when only one part is. The same goes for claims about a whole business when only one division qualifies. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses also stops companies from presenting legal minimums as special features. If the law requires recycled content in plastic packaging, brands cannot advertise it as a bonus. Honest marketing now means highlighting what goes beyond the rules. Misleading claims about product lifespan are also off limits. Companies cannot overstate how long a product lasts or claim it allows repairs when it doesn’t. They also cannot nudge shoppers to replace parts or refill consumables earlier than necessary. Sustainability labels face a new test. These rules apply to trust marks like Fairtrade, B Corp, and the Forest Stewardship Council. Labels must come from a public authority or a certification scheme that meets EU standards. An independent third party must verify that each scheme follows its standards. Businesses that display a label stay legally responsible for using only compliant ones. Labels that fail the test can no longer appear in the EU. Promises about the future need evidence. A company that says it will become carbon neutral needs a detailed plan with measurable, time-bound targets. An independent expert must review that plan regularly and share the findings with consumers. Sellers must also give buyers new information before a sale. Physical goods need a reminder about the two-year legal guarantee, using an EU template. Sellers must share details on repairs, spare parts, and software updates when available. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses requires companies promising future carbon neutrality to publish a detailed plan with measurable, time-bound targets reviewed regularly by an independent expert, while sellers must also give buyers information on the two-year legal guarantee, repairs, spare parts, and software updates. Photo by Sarah Chai on Pexels. Smartphones and tablets also need a repairability score. Online sellers must list environmentally friendly delivery options. National regulators in each EU country will enforce the EU greenwashing ban for businesses. Fines can reach 4% of yearly sales in that country, or more under national law. Claimants can also bring class-action-style cases under the Representative Actions Directive. Consider the scale of the 4% cap. A company with €50 million in sales in one country could face a €2 million fine. Accurate claims cost far less. The good news is that the EU greenwashing ban for businesses offers a clear path to compliance. Businesses can audit their websites, packaging, and ads for vague terms. Then they can swap broad slogans for specific, provable facts. Consider a hypothetical clothing brand. Instead of calling its jackets sustainable, it can name the exact share of recycled fabric. A verified label can then support that number. Each EU country writes its own national version of the rules, so details can vary. Germany, for example, limits its future claims rules to consumer sales. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses applies to any trader selling to EU customers, including online sellers. Businesses outside Europe that ship to EU customers should review their claims too. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses gives shoppers practical tools for choosing well. They can compare products using facts instead of vague slogans. They also learn more about repairs, spare parts, and warranties before buying. Companies can read the directive’s official text to see every requirement in detail. Reviewing it helps teams plan website updates and label changes. See also: Blockchain for a Greener Supply Chain: Transparency That Reduces Waste Readers who want to shop with confidence can also learn to spot greenwashing and greenhushing, when a company shares too little about real green efforts. Knowing both helps people judge vague environmental claims. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses rewards companies that do the real work. Shoppers gain a fairer way to judge what helps the planet. The post EU Greenwashing Ban for Businesses Puts Proof Behind Green Claims appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Κάποτε σπάνιο στο Ujani, 10 Lakh Deccan Mahseer Πάρτε μια νέα ευκαιρία μέσω ενός 10ετούς προγράμματος
items.titleOriginal: Once Rare in Ujani, 10 Lakh Deccan Mahseer Get a Fresh Chance Through a 10-Year Plan
items.description: Ένα ψάρι που είχε σχεδόν εξαφανιστεί από τη δεξαμενή Ujani της Μαχαράστρα πριν από δεκαετίες, έχει άλλη μια ευκαιρία να κολυμπήσει στα νερά της. items.descriptionOriginal: A fish that had nearly disappeared from Maharashtra's Ujani Reservoir decades ago is getting another chance to swim in its waters. The Deccan Mahseer, once found in abundance in the Bhima River basin, had become increasingly rare by the 1990s as pollution, invasive fish species and destructive fishing practices took a toll on the reservoir's native aquatic life. Now, in October 2026, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), with support from the Cipla Foundation and Tata Power, released 45 lakh (4.5 million) native fish fingerlings, including 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer (Tor khudree), popularly known as the 'Tiger of the River', alongside more than 21,000 aquatic plants into Maharashtra's Ujani wetland near Bhigwan. According to BNHS, the restoration programme responds to decades of ecological degradation in Ujani, where invasive fish, deteriorating water quality and destructive fishing practices have contributed to the decline of native species. Why did the fish disappear? Ujani Reservoir, formed by the Ujani Dam on the Bhima River, is an important freshwater ecosystem spanning parts of Pune, Solapur and Ahilyanagar districts. Over the years, however, its aquatic biodiversity has come under pressure from invasive fish, pollution and fishing methods that capture even young fish before they can reproduce. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. Photograph: (Rajeev Raghavan) Invasive species such as suckermouth catfish, tilapia and African catfish have spread through its waters. The BNHS-led restoration programme has also identified the impact of invasive aquatic vegetation , which can obstruct waterways, affect oxygen levels and compete with native plants. The scale of the intervention reflects the extent of the problem. BNHS and local fisheries societies have removed more than 178 tonnes of invasive fish from the reservoir over the past year. Additionally, nearly 6,500 tonnes of invasive vegetation, including water hyacinth, Ipomoea and Prosopis, have been cleared from approximately 2,000 hectares of the catchment area. The October stocking programme included 10 lakh Indian major carps, comprising rohu, catla and mrigal, alongside more than 22 lakh fingerlings of other native species, including kavdas, nukta and bobari. What makes the Deccan Mahseer important? The Deccan Mahseer, also known as the blue-fin mahseer, is a freshwater fish belonging to the carp family. Its historic distribution includes the Krishna River system and its tributaries across parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana. A 2019 scientific review, titled Mahseer (Tor spp.) Fishes of the World: Status, Challenges and Opportunities for Conservation , published in the journal Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries, examined the distribution, conservation status and threats facing mahseer species. This is the Deccan Mahseer, revered as Lord Vithoba's beloved "Devmaasa". Found in Indrayani river, it is now endangered due to pollution deadly water hyacinth growth on Anand Doha. A case of authorities' indifference😢 ##goodbadugly #saverivers Image: iNaturalist (1/2) https://t.co/5aTWC0UhK4 — Pune River Revival (@PuneRivers) May 22, 2024 The researchers identified the northern and central Western Ghats, particularly the Krishna River system, as the historical range of the Deccan Mahseer. Its tributaries include the Indrayani, Mula-Mutha, Koyna, Tungabhadra and Panchaganga. The review also highlighted how artificial propagation and large-scale fish stocking since the 1970s expanded the species' distribution beyond its original range. Some introduced populations have even shown invasive characteristics, affecting native fish populations in other river systems. Another study, published in Fisheries Research in 2011, examined the sustainability of Deccan Mahseer fisheries in the Western Ghats using catch data collected with the participation of local fishers. Researchers Rajeev Raghavan, Anvar Ali, Neelesh Dahanukar and Alison Rosser studied six fishing sites and found that catches frequently included immature fish. Their assessment also indicated that exploitation rates exceeded sustainable levels at most of the sites studied. A 10-year plan to bring the fish back The Ujani restoration programme included a dedicated partnership between BNHS and Tata Power for the conservation of the Deccan Mahseer. Under the arrangement, Tata Power has committed to supplying 10 lakh mahseer fingerlings over 10 years. The fish are being bred with support from its facility at Valvan in Lonavala. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BNHS 💚 Wildlife Conservation (@bombaynaturalhistorysociety) According to BNHS's October 2026 conservation newsletter, Dr Unmesh Katwate, head of the BNHS Wetland Eco-Restoration Project, visited the facility on 9 October to assess the available fingerling stock and preparations for their release. The newsletter also records a separate initial release of 8,000 fingerlings near Palasnath Temple in Ujani Reservoir on 22 October. The site was selected after considering its depth, water quality and habitat conditions. The organisation is also working with local fisheries societies and government departments to encourage more sustainable fishing practices. For Ujani, the return of the Deccan Mahseer is therefore part of a larger restoration exercise. Whether the mahseer can establish a self-sustaining population in the reservoir will become clearer through continued monitoring in the coming years. items.title: Από το πλύσιμο των πιάτων στο τραγούδι για εκατομμύρια: Ο Talwiinder λέει ειλικρινής για το πώς δίδαξε τον εαυτό του μουσική
items.titleOriginal: From Washing Dishes to Singing for Millions: Talwiinder Gets Candid About How He Taught Himself Music
items.description: Τι κάνεις όταν θέλεις να γίνεις μουσικός, αλλά το δοκιμαστήριο σου είναι ένα φαστ φουντ και ο χρόνος εξάσκησής σου ξεκινά αφού φύγει ο τελευταίος πελάτης; Για περισσότερα από τέσσερα χρόνια, η απάντηση του Talwiinder ήταν να τραγουδάει πλένοντας πιάτα και κλείνοντας το Subway. Άρχισε να εργάζεται εκεί στην Τάξη 10, προσαρμόζοντας το riyaaz (μουσική πρακτική) γύρω από την παραγγελία του πελάτη…
items.descriptionOriginal: What do you do when you want to become a musician, but your rehearsal room is a fast-food outlet and your practice time begins after the last customer has left? For more than four years, Talwiinder's answer was to sing while washing dishes and closing Subway. He started working there in Class 10, fitting riyaaz (music practice) around customer orders and closing duties. Without formal music training, he used the time after serving customers to practise his singing. Today, his music has travelled far beyond that counter. 'Pal Pal', made with Afusic and Ali Soomro, caught the attention of British DJ and producer Fred again.., who played the track during a livestream. Talwiinder saw it just like everyone else watching. It was, he says, "a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene". Between those closing shifts and the livestream were years of teaching himself music, writing songs and continuing to create despite rejection from music labels. From serving customers to writing songs Talwiinder has been singing since he was three or four, but he says the decision to build a life around music came when he began writing songs of his own. Singing was something he loved; songwriting gave that love somewhere to go . The 'Pal Pal' livestream moment connected a Punjabi collaboration with audiences beyond its listening community. Photograph: ( Instagram/@talwiinder ) "The moment I started to write my own songs, I knew I had to release these tracks for people who need it more than me," he tells The Better India . "Once I got into songwriting, I knew this is what I want to do for the rest of my life." There was no ready-made route into the industry. He spent more than four years at Subway, starting in Class 10, and remembers the job fondly for what it taught him about people. "It taught me communication, reading people's energy and having one-on-one conversations with customers to the point where I knew their whole order the moment they stepped in the store," he says. He learnt to run the store by himself. When the rush was over, he had time alone with his thoughts. "That alone time was often used to do riyaaz while cleaning dishes and closing the store," he says. "I loved every bit of that job and never felt like I wanted to quit." His music moves between Punjabi and international listening spaces, opening possibilities for cross-cultural collaboration. Interestingly, someone who once spent hours interacting with customers now prefers to keep conversations brief. He says he prefers texting to phone calls and often avoids conversations because talking for too long tires his throat and voice. He likes to "talk with eyes" and use very few words. He even has a WhatsApp display picture that reads, "Don't call me, text me." Through the songs he writes, however, Talwiinder communicates with millions of listeners. Learning how to express himself through music has involved years of listening to and understanding his own voice. How he taught himself music Without formal music training, Talwiinder learnt by making songs and returning to them. He advises beginners with a laptop or computer to invest in a home-recording setup, which he estimates can cost around $150 to $200, rather than waiting for a professional studio or teacher. "Record yourself as much as you can," he says. "You will understand your voice better. When the time comes and you're in a proper studio with top-notch equipment, you won't be so lost, but excited to go full beast mode." For listeners discovering Punjabi music abroad, Talwiinder offers an entry point into Punjabi sounds. Listening to these recordings helps a singer recognise what needs work and gradually develop a sound of their own. It is something aspiring musicians can begin doing with basic equipment at home. Over time, Talwiinder has also learnt when to stop working on a song and let listeners hear it. He does not believe there is a magical point at which a track becomes perfect. "The song is never ready; there will always be something that can be added or taken out," he says. "You have to trust your gut and give your 100% in stitching the song together, and once it's out, make peace with it and move on to the next song." With every release comes a public tally of streams, views and likes, but Talwiinder says he has never made numbers the measure of his work. He recalls gaining more than four million Instagram followers in a month without paid promotions. He says he has never bought fake views or likes, or followed trends. His focus, he says, is on doing justice to the music, while listeners decide whether to return to it. When he does not feel like starting something new, he returns to his unfinished tracks. "I have way too many unfinished songs," he says. He chooses his favourites and starts finishing them, turning a creative block into a chance to reopen old work. When music labels turned him down The years were not without rejection. Talwiinder remembers approaching labels that did not want to associate with his music. Among the tracks he mentions is 'Khayaal'. The singer's visual aesthetic draws from alternative music culture rather than conventional Punjabi entertainment imagery. "They told me indirectly and did not want to associate with my music," he says. "Funny thing is I still see those labels coming back and asking to work together." He kept making music, including songs that did not immediately find their moment. 'Haseen' was written and recorded in 2019 but released six years later. He says he would not change his older music simply because he has grown as an artist. "I believe good music does not have an expiration date," he says. A song does not lose its value, in his view, because it has been waiting in a folder. With 'Pal Pal', Talwiinder experienced what it was like for his music to reach someone he had not expected. The collaboration with Afusic and Ali Soomro caught the attention of Fred again.. When the British DJ played the track during a livestream, Talwiinder did not hear about it through a label or a carefully arranged announcement. He saw it on the stream, like everybody else. "It caught me by surprise," he says. "It was a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene." With his signature face paint and unconventional styling, Talwiinder has carved out a recognisable space in contemporary music. Having experienced rejection himself, Talwiinder now wants to help other aspiring musicians find people they can work with. Asked what he would do if a young artist arrived with little money and no industry connections, Talwiinder says he would first listen. If the work felt genuine and original, he would connect the artist with his community and suggest collaborators, giving them somewhere to belong. For someone who spent years practising after work and learning to make music on his own, being able to offer another young artist a place to begin is something he now looks forward to.

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Υπάρχουν λίγα μεγαλύτερα συναισθήματα t…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Mark Schroeder , a professor of philosophy at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts, and Sciences, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . There are few greater feelings than the sense of heartfelt gratitude to another human being who has done you a solid. Sincere thanks and reciprocation are part of the glue that binds us in human relationships. But sometimes you’re just not feeling it. You know that you have benefited from what someone has done for you, but you don’t really feel grateful to them for doing it. Most teenagers go through this period with their parents. Maybe you take your partner or colleague for granted. For me, 14 years ago, it was my mother-in-law. She had upended her life to move from South Dakota to California to live with my wife and me to assist with childcare after our daughter was born; no other source of childcare fit with our demanding work schedules and my commute. She made a huge sacrifice that transformed our lives, but there were moments when I really struggled to feel grateful. Since that time, I’ve come to devote much of my research as a philosopher to studying how the way that we interpret each other as people shapes our relationships . That work has helped me to understand why I struggled to be grateful — and taught me a little bit about how to do better. Personal Gratitude I’ve found that the hardest part of feeling grateful to someone is the “to” part. It is one thing to be impersonally grateful that something happened and another thing to be personally grateful to someone for doing it. These are not the same. Both forms of gratitude require seeing something as a benefit. And they both require a humble recognition of how easily things could have been otherwise. When the rain ends a drought, an atheist can feel grateful that the tomatoes will survive. But the atheist isn’t grateful “to” anyone for the rain. AP Photo/Mahesh Kumar A Priests offer prayers to Varuna, the Hindu god of rain, as they stand in the Osman Sagar on the outskirts of Hyderabad, India, on July 16, 2013. Personal gratitude requires more than impersonal gratitude. It is an example of what the philosopher Peter Strawson calls a “participant” attitude : an attitude that we have toward people, but not toward things. And a large theme in my work is that participant attitudes such as gratitude involve giving someone credit for what the attitude responds to. But which benefits we give people credit for is complicated. As philosophers such as Tony Manela have argued, actions motivated primarily by money, self-interest, or insecurity don’t merit personal gratitude , even when they benefit you. Actions motivated by love, generosity, or concern, on the other hand — or other “pro-social” motives — do. Sometimes people fail to feel gratitude because they take someone for granted, not noticing how easily they could have done otherwise. This wasn’t my problem with my mother-in-law. It was obvious that she didn’t have to move across the country to live with us. But it was hard to avoid noticing that she had always wanted to live in California. Sometimes it is hard to feel grateful because of how we interpret someone’s motives. They could have done otherwise, but we don’t think their action was really “about us.” Bad Motives Are Easy to Find Sometimes ungenerous motives can help people to be generous. Your child’s kindergarten teacher isn’t a volunteer. They may be a naturally generous person — but still, they probably wouldn’t be working with your child on spelling, arithmetic, and handling adversity if they weren’t getting a paycheck. It’s still appropriate to be grateful to them. Their financial incentive to show up for work enables their generosity, rather than competing with it. svetikd—E+/Getty Images Your child’s teacher might be generous, but their job enables them to act on that generosity every day. Elementary school teachers are not alone. After all, people’s decisions are often driven by many factors: some that merit gratitude and others that don’t. So if you go looking for selfish motives, you are bound to find some . Take your partner, for example. They do something that benefits you: buying you flowers, filling your tank with gas, or finally taking their turn to wash the dishes. They are partly motivated by generosity, love, or communal spirit. But, as in any close relationship, sometimes they may be hoping to get something out of it : reciprocation, maybe, or getting you off their back. It matters which of these you interpret as their “true” motive: Seeing it one way opens you up to gratitude, while the other precludes it. What Are “True” Motives? The distinction between someone’s “true” motive and the other motives that enable it looks like the distinction between causes and enabling conditions . For example, when you drop a wine glass, the fragility of the glass enables the drop to cause the break, but it isn’t itself a cause of the break — the drop is. In the case of the falling glass, there’s a clear, objective answer to what caused the break and what merely enabled it. But I believe that relating to people is deeply different than understanding physical things. The key question in whether to be grateful to someone isn’t about which motives count as “causes.” It is about which cause we need to bring into focus in order to see the other person more clearly for who they are . See It Their Way In other words, it’s at least partly a matter of perspective. If someone does you a favor, but you know they’re hoping for something in return, you can see that as their “true” motive. But you don’t have to see it that way. Instead, you could see that motive as the condition they need for their generosity to thrive. Shifting perspectives isn’t easy. When you’re doubting someone’s motives , their lack of generosity can feel obvious. But it helps to remember that people tend to believe they’re acting generously . If you want to respond with gratitude, try seeing them as they see themselves. What if that doesn’t work? Well, the next best thing to being grateful to someone is being grateful for them. Starting there is a good way to remind yourself of why you value this relationship in the first place. And it can be enough to simply say “thanks” and mean it. RELATED: Here Are 7 Ways to Express and Increase Your Gratitude

items.descriptionOriginal: Family, friends, football – Turkey Day is many things, but food is always at the center. Making the best side dish for Thanksgiving can occasionally feel like playing against the clock. Do you know how to make it exactly like grandma did? How are you supposed to keep it at optimum serving temperature when the turkey still has an hour to go? And most importantly, will the final product get the approval of that one aunt who never seems to like anything? No playbook, however, has been as fiercely guarded as NFL coach Andy Reid’s secret recipe for mac-and-cheese . For years, football fans whispered about the Kansas City Chiefs coach’s legendary cheesy creation. Whenever reporters asked for details, he stayed notoriously tight-lipped. Could anyone make him give up his culinary game plan ? Players, coaches, even The Washington Post tried to crack the case . Now, journalist Pablo Torre has finally uncovered the full recipe. The tasty mystery behind the mac-and-cheese This cheesy journey began at an airport terminal in 2018. Writer Charles McDonald bumped into Reid , and the conversation turned to Thanksgiving food. McDonald says that Reid pulled up various recipes on his phone. Then the famous coach offhandedly mentioned that his creamy version of the pasta classic features seven different cheeses. In the video, he only lists six cheeses: fontina, mozzarella, parmesan, sharp cheddar, gouda, and gruyere. The mystery of the seventh cheese left fans obsessed with tracking down the final ingredient. Why football fans craved Coach Reid’s recipe Andy Reid is famous for much more than his trademark moustache. He’s known for drawing up clever offensive plays that lead to big wins on the field. His warm nature and love of comfort food made the mystery of the missing cheese all the more irresistible. Whenever Reid was pressed for more details, he kept fans guessing. He famously joked that he could not give away the secrets because he might open a restaurant. For eight long years, fans debated what the missing seventh cheese could be. That lingering curiosity turned a simple side dish into one of sports media’s favorite running jokes. The seventh cheese and the surprise ingredient Journalist and podcaster Pablo Torre decided it was time to crack the case once and for all. He teamed up with Charles McDonald , former Chiefs tackle Mitchell Schwartz , and celebrity chef David Chang . The investigation revealed the missing ingredient. It turned out to be something no one had considered before: Velveeta. According to Reid, a little bit of the processed cheese product helps keep the melted sauce smooth and cohesive. There was more, however. An additional secret ingredient! Instead of standard breadcrumbs, Reid tops the dish with crushed cornflakes mixed with melted butter. The crispy cereal topping adds a golden crunch that feels wonderfully unexpected. Paired with a butter-and-flour roux, warm milk and cream, and seasonings, the dish brings serious comfort, and Reid’s family and friends quickly devour it . When Torre and Chang cooked it up for a taste test, the flavors won them over. Even a world-class chef had to admit the cornflake twist worked. Bringing a football legend’s feast to your table After years of speculation, home cooks can finally try the full recipe for themselves. It takes a little prep work, especially grating all those different cheeses. Still, the payoff is a rich, bubbly pan built for big holiday gatherings. Whether you make it straight from Reid’s notes or add your own spin, someone finally solves the mystery . Thanksgiving tables everywhere just got a lot cheesier. The post Andy Reid’s legendary secret mac-n-cheese recipe has finally been shared with the world appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Holiday season energy is officially here. Soon, the sounds of sleigh bells and Ho-ho-hoing Santas will fill every shopping center you walk into . And chances are good that you’ll hear the festive “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” pumping out of the mall’s speakers at least once. The singer, Brenda Lee, was only a tween when she recorded the perennial classic. Decades later, the song continues to climb the charts every December. Now it has earned a massive RIAA Diamond certification for surpassing 10 million copies . To mark the historic milestone, music superstar Taylor Swift surprised the 81-year-old legend in person. The heartwarming meetup brought Lee to tears. A heartfelt surprise between two music icons Seeing Taylor Swift present a gleaming Diamond plaque to Brenda Lee on behalf of the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) is a true gift to music fans. The song is an enduring holiday classic for sure, but there are even deeper connections between Swift and Lee. They both started young and began their recording careers in Tennessee. Swift’s debut album arrived when she turned 16 , while Lee was only 12. There’s plenty about this musician meet-cute that will bring a smile to your face. Especially Lee’s adorable astonishment at Taylor Swift’s height. When wearing heels, Swift is six feet tall. But the real emotion comes after Brenda Lee receives the Diamond Certification. She tears up as she mentions the song’s writer, Johnny Marks . You probably know his two other seasonal classics, “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” and “A Holly Jolly Christmas.” The song reached #1 on the Billboard charts again in 2023 . That made her the oldest woman to ever reach the top spot. “This is yours now, and it will be yours forever,” Swift tells an emotional Lee. Taylor also refers to Lee as “the original queen of Christmas.” Only one modern Christmas song reached Diamond status before “Rockin’…” That being Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Brenda Lee’s remarkable rise and holiday chart magic Brenda Lee’s story makes this milestone even more extraordinary . As a young child, she possessed a powerhouse voice. She only began singing professionally, however, after the death of her father. Lee sang at county fairs and on local TV to help earn money for her family. Soon after, she signed a record deal at Decca at 12 years old. Known affectionately as “Little Miss Dynamite,” Lee broke through in the late 1950s. She moved effortlessly between rockabilly, pop, and country music long before genre lines blurred. Her vocal grit and emotional maturity stunned listeners. Songs like “I’m Sorry” cemented her place as an unforgettable vocal force. Lee was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1997 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2002. Meanwhile, “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” is an annual chart phenomenon. Modern Billboard rules count both classic catalog songs and holiday tracks. And since streaming and radio play surge every winter, old favorites can suddenly sprint back toward No. 1 during peak holiday weeks. In Lee’s case, Spotify announced in 2024 that “Rockin’…” had crossed the one billion stream mark in 2024. Why this timeless classic still warms our hearts Music has a unique ability to freeze moments in time. A familiar guitar riff or joyful lyric can transport us straight back to a Christmas of your childhood. Lee’s song is part of a trio of tracks that were the first to merge holiday music with rock and roll beats . Bobby Helm’s “Jingle Bell Rock” came out of the gate swinging in 1957. That was followed the next year by Lee’s “Rockin’…” and Chuck Berry’s “Run Rudolph Run” —which leapt quickly onto the charts. It’s a seasonal formula that many of today’s recording artists try to replicate. Just this year, Olivia Rodrigo made a splash with “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” which evokes the New Wave sound of The Waitresses’ 1981 classic, “Christmas Wrapping.” What will always make Brenda Lee’s track so catchy is her youthful energy. Watching Taylor Swift honor such a trailblazer reminds us of what we love about the season. Family, friends, and holiday traditions set to a rockin’ beat for generations to come. The post Taylor Swift surprises 81-year-old Brenda Lee with RIAA Diamond plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: For many decades, Americans have debated Thanksgiving and the “first Thanksgiving” story, digging into the history versus the mythology of the Pilgrims and Native Americans breaking bread together. Some even shun the holiday to protest how the Thanksgiving origin story has been sanitized to obscure painful historical realities. The problem is that that hotly debated history is a myth within another myth, as the federal Thanksgiving holiday wasn’t originally tied to the Pilgrims, Native Americans, or Plymouth at all. Let’s unpack it. The first presidential Thanksgiving proclamation had zero mention of the Pilgrims Local Thanksgiving festivals had been observed in the U.S. long before it became a national holiday, often to give thanks for a successful harvest. But the official holiday is an entirely different thing. The first federal U.S. Thanksgiving holiday was proclaimed by George Washington in October of 1789 (which you can read here ). None of its over 450 words mention, or even allude to, the Pilgrims sitting down to feast with the Wampanoag people. Instead, Washington declared Thursday, November 26th, a holiday to give “sincere and humble thanks” to “that great and glorious Being, who is the beneficent Author of all the good that was, that is, or that will be” for bounties including the outcome of the Revolutionary War, the establishment of a constitutional government, the “civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed,” the ability to acquire knowledge, and the general blessings and favors of God. He also called for prayers asking God to pardon transgressions and bless the nation and all mankind. Nothing about the “first Thanksgiving” or anything related to that story. Lincoln made Thanksgiving an annual holiday. He also made no mention of the Pilgrims. Thanksgiving became an annual federal holiday with Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation naming the last Thursday in November an official day of Thanksgiving. The nation was in the middle of the Civil War, and Lincoln’s Thanksgiving proclamation spoke of the many things that were going well in the United States despite the ongoing military conflict. Something deeply moving about Lincoln making Thanksgiving a national holiday in the midst of the Civil War because we may “expect continuance of years with large increase of freedom” and “God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy.” pic.twitter.com/j5oFyPNeac — Phil Klay (@PhilKlay) November 25, 2025 “No human counsel hath devised nor hath any mortal hand worked out these great things,” the proclamation read. “They are the gracious gifts of the Most High God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy. It has seemed to me fit and proper that they should be solemnly, reverently and gratefully acknowledged as with one heart and one voice by the whole American People.” Lincoln also called for Americans to pray for the loved ones of those lost in the war, and to implore the Almighty “to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with the Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquillity and Union.” But again, nothing about Pilgrims or Native Americans or Plymouth. Lincoln created Thanksgiving to unite the U.S. during its bloodiest war. (In fact, Southerners resisted the Thanksgiving holiday , seeing it as Yankee abolitionist propaganda.) No president associated the Pilgrims with Thanksgiving until 1939—and that was just a brief mention Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving to the fourth Thursday of November instead of the last in 1939, when the last Thursday of November fell on the 30th, which created a late start to the holiday shopping season. Congress took the president’s lead and issued a resolution in 1941 , establishing the holiday as we know it today, on the fourth Thursday. In 1939, FDR moved Thanksgiving to the second to last Thursday of November. However, 16 states refused to accept the proclamation. It wasn't until Congress passed a resolution in 1941 that all states celebrated Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November. #Thanksgiving pic.twitter.com/JH7ifGtkr5 — American History TV (@cspanhistory) November 24, 2022 FDR’s 1939 Thanksgiving proclamation was the first to mention the Pilgrims, but even then, it wasn’t tied to any Pilgrim-Native “first Thanksgiving” meal. “More than three centuries ago at the season of the gathering in of the harvest, the Pilgrims humbly paused in their work and gave thanks to God for the preservation of their community and for the abundant yield of the soil,” FDR said. That’s it. That was the first official Pilgrim connection to the federal Thanksgiving holiday, and it came nearly six decades after it was established. So how did we end up with the ‘first Thanksgiving’ story and subsequent myth-busting? The tying of Thanksgiving to the image of a friendly feast between the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag (ignoring the complicated reality and history that followed) evolved primarily after the federal holiday was established. Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of the popular women’s periodical Godey Lady’s Book from 1837 until 1877, had made a relentless push for a national Thanksgiving holiday, petitioning five presidents before Lincoln finally made it happen. She called it a “good old puritan custom” in her pitch to make it a holiday, but she envisioned more of a Christian day of prayer rather than a big celebratory food feast. She did offer recipes for seasonal foods such as turkey and cranberry sauce, however, and her connecting the holiday to New England history and traditions planted the seed for modern Thanksgiving mythology. The widespread tie-in to the “first Thanksgiving” between the Pilgrims and Native Americans was driven largely by panic over immigration in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. People were worried about assimilation as a wave of immigrants arrived in the U.S., and a narrative of American identity emerged through a revised origin of the Thanksgiving holiday. As the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History writes, “The holiday was secularized during the last decades of the [19th] century, and by the twentieth century, costumed festivals honoring the Pilgrims became themes of elaborate grade-school pageants—an effective way to ‘Americanize’ immigrants. These annual activities showcased Puritan values and Yankee customs, promoting civic folk rituals.” Since then, it’s stuck. The history of colonists and indigenous peoples is important—it’s just not what Thanksgiving was about The way the story of Thanksgiving has played out has led to woeful inaccuracies and painful erasures of indigenous people’s experiences in American history. Because of that, the fact that the national Thanksgiving holiday wasn’t even based on that story adds yet another layer of complexity to conversations around celebrating it. On one hand, it means we can honestly make the holiday broadly about gratitude, as the original federal proclamations did. On the other hand, discussions of the historical inaccuracies surrounding the “first Thanksgiving” have been, and continue to be, important. Nothing about correcting the record on the official federal holiday origin erases the need for those conversations. In fact, it’s a good reminder that they need to be had regularly, not just once a year on a holiday whose origin has been muddled in so many ways. The post The origin of the Thanksgiving holiday actually had nothing to do with the Pilgrims or Native Americans appeared first on Upworthy .

Η κοινή γνώμη άρχισε να αλλάζει τη δεκαετία του 1990, καθώς οι εναλλακτικές και πανκ ροκ υποκουλτούρες έπληξαν το mainstream και ακόμη και τους στρέιτ φολκ σταρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you went back in time to the 1980s , one of the biggest changes you’d notice is the lack of tattoos. It’s estimated that in the ’80s, around 10% of the American population was tatted, as compared to 32% today. Public opinion began to shift in the 1990s as alternative and punk rock subcultures hit the mainstream and even straight-laced folks started getting inked. In the ‘90s, tattoos shifted from a symbol of gangs, the military, or dangerous subcultures to an art form, with the rise of superstar tattoo artists such as Ed Hardy and Mr. Cartoon . Another big cultural shift during this time was that women made up a large number of those embracing the new body aesthetic. Tattoos have reached the mainstream, and visible ink is now acceptable in many professions where it used to be forbidden, so these days, body art doesn’t seem intimidating. However, a new study by Farid Pazhoohi, Ph.D., published in Evolutionary Psychological Science found that tattoos still make people a little uncomfortable. Why We Might Give Tattooed Strangers a Little More Room | Farid Pazhoohi Ph D, Psychology Today New research finds that tattoos subtly shape comfort and attractiveness ratings. Picture two people standing in line ahead of you. They look identical, except that one has visible… pic.twitter.com/r2ZK5UGxMu — Owen Gregorian (@OwenGregorian) November 21, 2026 In the study, people were shown computer-generated images of people with or without tattoos, and they found that those without tattoos made them more comfortable. “People generally felt slightly more comfortable with the non-tattooed figures than with their tattooed counterparts,” Pazhoohi wrote in Psychology Today . “The average comfort ratings were approximately 5.12 versus 4.95 on a seven-point scale. The difference was small but statistically significant, and it appeared for both male and female figures.” It’s interesting that some are still uncomfortable around people with tattoos, given how prevalent they are. But it’s good news for those who got inked to look edgier and more intimidating—your body art still works on some people. A tattoo artist doing their job. Credit: Canva The study found that for those who are intimidated, it doesn’t matter how close the person is to them. “Although participants felt more comfortable as the distance increased, the effect of tattoos did not significantly change with distance,” Pazhoohi wrote. “This suggests that tattoos may influence our general impression of someone rather than specifically making us uncomfortable when that person gets too close.” Another interesting takeaway is that the study found men and women have differing opinions on whether tattoos make someone more attractive. “Male participants rated both male and female figures as more attractive when they did not have tattoos. Female participants, however, showed no significant difference in attractiveness ratings between tattooed and non-tattooed figures,” Pazhoohi continues. A woman getting a ttoo on her thigh. Credit: Canva Ultimately, the study shows that even though tattoos have become nearly ubiquitous in modern society, they can still affect how we perceive others without knowing anything else about them. “What I find particularly interesting is that participants knew nothing about the figures they were judging. They had no information about their personalities, backgrounds, or behaviour,” Pazhoohi wrote. “Yet changing one visible feature was enough to influence their ratings. It is a small example of something much broader: how readily we form impressions of others based on appearance, often without knowing why.” The post Tattoos have become as American as apple pie. But it turns out they still make people nervous. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Sixty years ago, The Monkees released “I’m a Believer,” which became the group’s biggest hit, spending a remarkable seven consecutive weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100. And of course, musical talent aside, the band certainly had Neil Diamond to thank, since he wrote the song. Only Diamond originally envisioned a much different singer to bring the song to life. “I’m a Believer”…as a country song? In 1966, Diamond was in New York, on the precipice of a breakthrough as a solo songwriter, following the success of his single “Cherry, Cherry .” During this time, Diamond wrote “I’m a Believer,” which he considered for country music crooner Eddy Arnold, known for “Make the World Go Away.” Not exactly the upbeat, radio-friendly pop group The Monkees would become. However, music executive Don Kirshner steered the song to The Monkees instead, with Micky Dolenz singing lead vocals and Jeff Barry as the producer. And the timing of that decision couldn’t have worked out any better. When “I’m a Believer” was released, the Monkees’ self-titled sitcom premiered on NBC, and their debut single, “Last Train to Clarksville,” had reached No. 1 on the Hot 100. The Monkees had a pretty incredible run with it “I’m a Believer” quickly became one of the defining songs of the decade and helped establish The Monkees as something much bigger than a fictional band created for television. Not to mention, it became one of Diamond’s most celebrated songwriting achievements. A win-win all around. But the song’s story didn’t end with the 1960s. Diamond eventually recorded his own version in 1971, and other artists have put their own spins on the song over the years. Then Smash Mouth gave it another life One of its biggest second lives came in 2001, when Smash Mouth recorded “I’m a Believer” for the soundtrack to Shrek . Their version reached No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100, giving the 35-year-old song another run on the charts. The cover became one of the most recognizable musical moments from the movie, helping cement Smash Mouth’s version alongside The Monkees’ original in pop culture. For younger listeners, the song suddenly had a whole new context, one that had nothing to do with a 1960s sitcom. Dolenz looks back on “I’m a Believer” 60 years later In celebration of the song’s 60th anniversary, Dolenz, the last surviving member of The Monkees, shared a heartfelt Instagram tribute commending the various artists who came together to bring it to life. View this post on Instagram “A lot of wonderful people helped create that sound. Stan Free played the unmistakable organ part, Artie Butler handled the arrangement, and Neil himself played acoustic guitar on the session.” Dolenz also reflected on what the song has meant to him after performing it countless times over the years. “I’ve sung that song more times than I could ever count, and it still means a great deal to me. It’s the song we close every show with, and there’s something incredibly special about hearing a whole room sing it back. No matter where we play, that moment always gets me,” he added. “If you’re lucky, a few songs become part of your life. For me, ‘I’m a Believer’ is one of those.” The post Neil Diamond wrote The Monkees’ biggest hit, but they weren’t his first choice to sing it appeared first on Upworthy .
