items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How to Reduce Waste When Renovating Your Home Reading Time: 3 minutes Renovating can make your home work better for you, but stripping out rooms and replacing old materials can create a lot of waste along the way. In England alone, 63.3 million tonnes of non-hazardous construction and demolition waste were generated in 2024, according to UK statistics on waste . Your individual renovation will only represent a tiny part of that picture, but it still makes sense to question what you throw away. Keeping useful features, finding new homes for unwanted materials and buying with longevity in mind can all make a refurbishment less wasteful. Work with what you already have A renovation does not have to start with an empty room. Before removing anything, look at what you already have and decide whether each feature genuinely needs replacing or simply needs some attention. Kitchen units offer a good example. If the carcasses remain sturdy, you could keep them and change the doors or handles instead. Wooden flooring can often be sanded and refinished, while dated furniture may look completely different after a repair or a fresh coat of paint. Keeping existing features can make financial sense too. When you avoid unnecessarily replacing a perfectly usable item, you can put that part of your budget towards improvements that matter more to you. It also helps to separate function from appearance. Something may no longer suit the style you have in mind, but that does not necessarily make it waste. Painting or repairing it could achieve the result you want without buying a brand-new replacement. Find another use for what you remove You will not be able to keep everything, particularly during a larger renovation. However, removing an item from your home does not automatically mean you need to put it in a skip. Doors, cabinets, shelves and unopened building materials could potentially find a second home. You might sell suitable pieces through Facebook Marketplace or eBay, offer them through Freecycle, or contact a local reclamation yard to see what it accepts. Think about this before demolition begins. Once someone throws reusable materials into a skip alongside rubble and broken plasterboard, you may find it much harder to recover them in a usable condition. You can also keep certain leftover materials for future repairs. A few spare bathroom tiles take up very little storage space, for example, but could prove useful if one cracks several years after you finish the renovation. The same applies to a small amount of correctly labelled paint or spare flooring. Be selective about what you replace Sometimes replacing an old fitting is unavoidable. It may leak, perform poorly or simply have reached the end of its useful life. However, renovating gives you an opportunity to think more carefully about what genuinely needs to go. In a kitchen, you might replace damaged worktops while keeping a perfectly usable sink, or change cupboard fronts without removing the units behind them. If you do need new kitchen taps , choosing a style that works with the finished room can sit alongside practical considerations such as water efficiency and build quality. You can use the same thinking throughout your home. A higher-quality fitting that you can maintain or repair may stay in place considerably longer than a cheaper alternative that you have to replace when one component fails. Try to consider the expected lifespan of an item alongside its upfront price. Spending a little more on something durable may reduce the number of times you need to buy, remove and dispose of the same type of product in the future. Avoid creating waste with new materials Renovation waste does not only come from old materials. Ordering too much of something can leave you with boxes of tiles, excess timber or unused flooring once the work finishes. Measure the space carefully before ordering and calculate how much material the project realistically requires. You will usually need to allow some extra for cuts, breakages and mistakes, but that is different from ordering a large surplus simply to be safe. It is worth checking a retailer’s returns policy before you buy as well. If it accepts unused full packs, you have the option of returning excess materials rather than storing them indefinitely or throwing them away. You may also find ways to use smaller leftovers around the home. Timber offcuts could become a shelf, while a handful of spare tiles might be enough for a small splashback or another repair. Creating a more sustainable home is not only about adding new eco-friendly products . Sometimes the greener decision is to keep something for longer, repair what you can and think about where materials will end up before you remove them. With a little more planning, you can still create a home that feels different without treating everything that came before as disposable. The post How to Reduce Waste When Renovating Your Home appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work Reading Time: 4 minutes How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work There are more than 100 million annual bird sightings logged on eBird by observers every day, yet many nature enthusiasts still assume meaningful conservation work requires formal lab credentials and massive institutional budgets. A lingering gap between public curiosity and formal scientific access often leaves local ecosystems unmonitored for years. Citizen science bridges that divide by turning routine outdoor observations into structured ecological data. Worldwide, conservation agencies, universities, and wildlife nonprofits now actively recruit everyday observers to track species shifts, flag habitat loss, and expand research capacity far beyond what small field teams could manage alone. What Citizen Science Is and Why It Matters Citizen science invites members of the public to collect, classify, and share real-world observations with professional researchers. Rather than replacing trained ecologists, public contributors act as an expansive sensory network across neighborhoods, coastlines, and rural landscapes. Small academic teams rarely have the budget to monitor thousands of square miles simultaneously. Volunteers fill those geographic and seasonal blind spots simply by documenting what lives in their backyards or along familiar trails. Even a single timestamped photograph of a blooming wildflower or migrating raptor adds an anchor point to regional biodiversity maps. How Volunteer Data Informs Habitat Protection and Species Management Raw sightings only become useful when researchers can aggregate them into clear ecological patterns. Once uploaded to shared repositories, thousands of individual logs reveal when migratory birds arrive early, where invasive plants are spreading, or which amphibian populations are quietly declining. Wildlife managers rely on these trends to prioritize land acquisition and adjust seasonal protections. Here’s an example. When volunteer records consistently show pollinators clustering along a specific utility corridor, municipal planners gain concrete evidence to preserve that strip instead of mowing it down. Accurate local records turn vague environmental concern into defensible policy decisions. Turning Field Curiosity into a Conservation Career Spending weekends logging water quality or tracking nesting shorebirds frequently changes how people view their own professional lives. Casual curiosity sharpens into methodical questioning once an observer starts noticing why certain species thrive in one creek and vanish from the next. Many volunteers discover they want more than a weekend hobby. Moving from enthusiast to full-time practitioner usually requires structured academic preparation. Inspired participants explore options ranging from technical field certifications to formal biology degree programs that build the scientific foundation needed for careers in wildlife research, environmental policy, and conservation management. Coursework in ecology, genetics, and statistical analysis equips aspiring conservationists to design the very studies they once supported as volunteers. Partnering with Schools, Nonprofits, and Conservation Organizations Individual data collection carries real weight, yet institutional partnerships multiply what a single observer can accomplish. Local schools, land trusts, and watershed coalitions frequently coordinate regional monitoring drives that align volunteer effort with urgent research gaps. Community groups can amplify their conservation footprint through several collaborative pathways: K-12 classrooms adopt nearby streams to submit seasonal macroinvertebrate counts to state environmental agencies Regional land trusts pair amateur naturalists with staff biologists for annual breeding bird inventories Municipal park departments host weekend BioBlitz events to catalog urban tree health and insect diversity University extension offices train community volunteers to monitor invasive species along public trail systems Working inside an organized network ensures that observations follow standardized protocols, making the resulting datasets far more reliable for peer-reviewed analysis. How Community Involvement Builds Local Stewardship People rarely fight to protect landscapes they barely know. Regularly surveying a neighborhood wetland or coastal dune creates an intimate familiarity that abstract news headlines never match. Once residents recognize individual warbler species or spot early signs of soil erosion, conservation stops feeling like someone else’s responsibility. Neighbors begin attending zoning hearings, advocating for native landscaping, and mentoring younger observers. Shared fieldwork transforms passive bystanders into vocal stewards who hold local leaders accountable for environmental decisions. Popular Citizen Science Projects and Monitoring Tools Getting involved does not require specialized laboratory equipment or remote expedition travel. Modern mobile platforms and long-running seasonal counts make participation accessible from almost anywhere. Birdwatchers frequently contribute to global avian databases during annual backyard counts, logging species abundance across winter and spring migrations. Pollinator enthusiasts use dedicated survey protocols to record bumblebee and monarch activity in community gardens. Meanwhile, smartphone wildlife apps allow hikers to snap photos of butterflies , fungi, reptiles, and plants, using computer vision paired with community verification to confirm the identities of species within hours. Measuring Long-Term Conservation Impact Skeptics sometimes wonder whether crowd-sourced observations hold up under rigorous scientific scrutiny. Over the past decade, researchers have developed robust validation frameworks that filter outliers and verify identification accuracy. Recent evaluations show that adaptable volunteer monitoring protocols help conservation scientists respond quickly to shifting ecological priorities without sacrificing data integrity. In marine and coastal regions, international bodies have also established clear quality labeling and sharing standards so community-gathered ocean datasets integrate smoothly into global climate assessments. Longitudinal records spanning ten or twenty years now underpin major habitat restoration grants and endangered species reviews. Getting Started in Your Local Community Stepping into citizen science works best when you start small and stay consistent. Choose a single taxon or local habitat you already enjoy visiting, then commit to observing it across changing seasons. Researchers consistently find that structured community-based biodiversity monitoring yields the strongest conservation value when participants stick with simple, repeatable reporting routines. Choosing a Local Focus Area Start with a nearby park, creek, or backyard garden rather than planning ambitious weekend expeditions. Familiarity with one small patch makes it much easier to spot subtle ecological shifts over time. Learning Basic Observation Protocols Spend twenty minutes reviewing how a project records location, weather, and species counts before submitting your first entry. Clean metadata matters just as much as a sharp photograph when scientists analyze your logs later. Connecting with Regional Coordinators Reach out to a local nature center, watershed alliance, or birding club to ask which datasets regional managers actually need. Aligning your walks with active local priorities ensures your notes solve real conservation problems. Where Everyday Observation Meets Lasting Stewardship Citizen science proves that meaningful environmental protection does not belong exclusively to credentialed specialists. Every careful observation adds another verifiable thread to our collective understanding of changing ecosystems. Whether you stay an active neighborhood volunteer or pursue formal scientific training, consistent attention to the natural world creates tangible momentum for conservation. If this piece was helpful, explore more guides on environmental conservation, field research, and community stewardship across our related articles below. items.descriptionOriginal: A bird following a boat at sea can mean a variety of things to superstitious sailors. They have been seen as harbingers of nearby land, bearers of the souls of the dead or talismans of good luck, among others. Now add this: They deliver data. A group of scientists from the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Spain have wired seabirds with tiny audio recorders and used them as unwitting boat-trackers. The recordings reveal these birds are encountering a lot more vessels on the water than regular vessel-monitoring systems show, according to a paper published today in Science Advances . That insight could help conservationists better protect endangered seabirds from getting killed by fishing nets. “For threatened seabirds,” said Jonathan Rutter , a University of Oxford scientist and the paper’s lead author. “Understanding where they encounter fishing vessels is crucial to protecting them.” Fishing boats can be a magnet for seabirds seeking an easy meal from trapped or discarded fish. But those encounters can prove lethal for animals like the Balearic shearwater , considered Europe’s most endangered seabird . Accidental capture by fishing nets or lines, commonly known as bycatch, is a prime threat to the gull-like brown bird that nests only on Spain’s Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean Sea. That makes knowing the whereabouts of fishing boats a key part of protecting and recovering such birds. It can help scientist estimate the toll of bycatch, and whether measures such as fishing restrictions are needed. But it’s hard to know how many boats are really on the water. Most large vessels are supposed to carry transponders that continuously signal their location. But there has long been a problem with “invisible” boats, because beacons are turned off or malfunctioning, or sailors eschew the equipment altogether. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , crisscrossed by 1000s of ships that have been virtually invisible. Until now. Some researchers have used satellites to try to solve the problem . But that doesn’t tell scientists how much birds are interacting with these boats. The advent of small, cheap audio recorders and computer programs capable of identifying the acoustic fingerprint of various animals and machines gave Rutter and colleagues another approach. They attached acoustic recorders and tracking devices to seabirds in three different parts of the ocean to see what boats they encountered. In the North Atlantic near the British Isles they used seven northern gannets. In the Mediterranean near the Spanish coast they outfitted four Balearic shearwaters. And in the south Pacific they used a lone Westland petrel. The audio recordings revealed that the birds encountered far more vessels than standard tracking data revealed. The tell-tale drone of ship equipment, compared to vessel tracking records, told the scientists that roughly 57% of the gannets’ ship encounters occurred with vessels that didn’t turn up in normal monitoring systems. For shearwaters, it was around 20%. “We know that seabirds regularly interact with fishing vessels at sea, but what surprised us was just how many of these interactions were missing from conventional tracking records,” said Rutter. The system isn’t perfect. It could be fine-tuned to better distinguish the sounds of fishing boats from other craft. And it wouldn’t work in cases where fishers string lines of hooks stretching dozens of kilometers across the water, far out of earshot of the boat. The method “is not a silver bullet,” the authors write. But it could be “a growing toolbox in which no method provides a complete picture.” So don’t expect flocks of eavesdropping birds to suddenly take to the skies. Then again, these days you never know who’s listening. Rutter et. al. “Unseen but not unheard: Animal-borne audio recorders reveal missing interactions between seabirds and untracked vessels.” Science Advances. Nov. 25, 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: Childhood dishes can take you straight back to your seat at the family dinner table. Comfort meals that were served there are uber-nostalgic. And there is one dish that represents the epitome of Gen X and baby boomer childhoods: casseroles. These one-dish wonders were loaded with flavor and baked to perfection. Pulled straight from the oven to the dinner table, casseroles filled the house with the smell of unique home-cooked recipes. And while most of us are eating casseroles today at Thanksgiving , Gen Xers and boomers grew up eating casseroles on the reg. Here are 15 old-school casserole recipes that Redditors grew up eating, which are just as yummy today: Chicken casseroles Fancy Fast Chicken casserole “ Fancy Fast Chicken is delicious and so simple. Line up chicken breasts in a casserole dish. Dump uncooked stuffing over top the chicken breasts. Pour Cream of Mushroom (Onion or chicken works too) and incorporate it into the stuffing. Top with cheese of your choice, and fried onions if you’re inclined. Bake at 350 for 45min or until chicken is thoroughly cooked.” – Applepoisoneer Chicken Curry Divan casserole “My favorite is Chicken Curry Divan. A friend made it for me in college 40 years ago and it is a favorite to this day. Never disappoints. Many people have asked me for the recipe over the years. My best friends kids now that they are grown have each approached me for it. 1 1/2 lbs chicken breast tenders cooked and cut into bite sized pieces 3 cups broccoli in bite sized pieces 2 cans Cream of Chicken soup 1 cup mayonnaise (must be Mayo) 2 tsp curry Juice of 1 lemon Shredded sharp cheddar (use the amount you like o like a nice even cover of the top) 3/4 cup crushed Ritz crackers 3 tbsp melted butter In 9×13” baking pan layer chicken then broccoli. Mix the soup, Mayo, lemon juice and curry together well, pour over chicken broccoli mixture evenly and smooth out. Sprinkle cheese over top evenly. Crush crackers fine, mix in melted butter well and sprinkle evenly over top. Cook at 375° for 25-30 minutes until bubbly and top brown. Serve with rice.” – karinchup Chicken and Rice casserole “This baked rice & cheese casserole has become a staple in our house! It’s great as a side dish, or I’ll add rotisserie chicken and serve it as a main dish.” – anchovypepperonitoni Chicken & Dumplings casserole “The secret of this is not to stir anything. That’s what makes your dumplings. When you dish it out, you have your dumplings on top. 2 chicken breasts, cooked and shredded; 2 cups chicken broth; 1/2 stick of butter; 2 cups Bisquick mix; 2 cups whole milk; 1 can cream of chicken soup; 1/2 medium onion, minced; 1 cup frozen peas; 3 tsp chicken Better Than Bouillon; 1/2 tsp dried sage; 1 tsp black pepper; 1/2 tsp salt. (1) Preheat oven to 350 degrees (2) Layer 1 – In 9×13 casserole dish, melt 1/2 stick of butter. Spread shredded chicken over butter. Sprinkle black pepper and dried sage over this layer. Do not stir. (3) Layer 2 – Sprinkle minced onions and peas over chicken (4) Layer 3 – In small bowl, mix milk and Bisquick. Slowly pour all over chicken. Do not stir. (5) Layer 4 – In medium bowl, whisk together 2 cups of chicken broth, chicken bouillon, and soup. Once blended, slowly pour over the Bisquick layer. Do not stir. (6) Bake casserole for 30-40 minutes, or until the top is golden brown.” – Superb_Yak7074 Chicken broccoli casserole “I made chicken broccoli casserole last week and that’s a favorite here. This is pretty close to how I do it.” – gimmethelulz Potato casseroles Funeral Potatoes “The unfortunately named, funeral potatoes !” – IRLperson Tater Tot casserole “ Tater tot casserole . My mom made this at least once a week when I was growing up, but she added a quart of green beans to make it a meal. If you brown your ground beef in a good size cast iron skillet, you only dirty up one pan to make it!” – hcynthia1234, upperwareParTAY Breakfast casserole “I’m making a breakfast casserole this morning for brunch later, a bag of frozen hash brown potatoes thawed, a pound of sausage sauteed with peppers and onions, a brick of cheese grated, eight eggs beaten with a bit of milk and cream and some salt and pepper. Layer in a casserole, ending with cheese. Bake around an hour at 375.” – CWrend Hamburger pie casserole “One of my childhood favorites . Did not add vegetables or cheese though. This was an end of the month struggle meal that everyone loved.” – DarnHeather Shepherd’s pie casserole “Shepherd’s pie : brown 1.5 lbs ground beef with half a chopped onion, salt and pepper, drain it and then spread into a 13×9 and stir a can of cream of mushroom soup into it. Spread a drained family size can of corn on top, use a container of prepared mashed potatoes for the top layer. Bake for a half hour at 350.” – ExplanationLucky1143 Noodle casseroles Tuna casserole “Love my mom’s tuna noodle casserole: 1 bag broad egg noodles, 1 can cream of mushroom soup, 2 cans tuna, 1 cup frozen corn or 1 can kernel corn, 2 cups shredded sharp cheddar cheese, 1/2 cup seasoned bread crumbs, 1 tbsp celery salt Cook noodles per package directions, drain, then place in a 13×9 casserole dish. Mix in cream of mushroom soup, tuna, corn, 1 cup of the cheddar cheese, and celery salt. Top the casserole with the remaining cheese and bread crumbs. Bake at 350 for 20 minutes or until done enough for you.” – Pinkleton Mock Stroganoff casserole “Mock stroganoff – brown 1lb ground chuck. Mix in 8 oz sour cream and 1 can cream of mushroom. Add to 1 lb of cooked egg noodles. Season with black pepper. Extras – fresh mushrooms and/or onion cooked with the beef. Any precooked veggies of your choice, peas or broccoli work well. Splash of Worcestershire, soy sauce, or fish sauce. Garlic or onion powder. Parsley, thyme, or cilantro.” – Nathan_Saul Cabbage noodle casserole “I have a quick cabbage and noodles that uses bagged cole slaw. Cook a bag of noodles. Put aside. Cut up a lb of bacon and a med onion. Cook in pan until bacon is slightly fried and onions are clear. Add cabbage(without carrots) let sit 10 min or so. Add to noodles. It’s so easy.” – conjas11 Vegetable casseroles Green bean casserole “ This is the best green bean casserole recipe, it does use the canned onions but you make your own cream of mushroom and it’s soooo good. I’ve made it on random weekends, it’s not just a Thanksgiving food. I don’t know much about older foods, I just really wanted to share that recipe.” Corn casserole “Our family Corn custard doesn’t have crackers but we double the recipe and there’s never any left over. 2 eggs, 1 cup of sweetened condensed milk, 1/2 flour, 2 T soft butter, 1 tsp sugar, 1 can of creamed corn, 1 can of whole corn. Mix all together and bake in a 8×8 about 45 min at 350. Gotta have that!” – Psychological_Bat890 What are your easy casserole week night recipes by u/arifirari in Old_Recipes Casseroles still have a spot at the table Casseroles started as budget-friendly dinners, but they stuck around because they work: one dish, simple ingredients, and enough to feed everyone. For many Gen Xers and boomers, they also taste like childhood. Thanksgiving is this Thursday, so there’s a good chance one of these recipes will make it onto your table, whether it’s the green bean classic or a pan of funeral potatoes. Which casserole did you grow up eating? Tell us in the comments. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post 15 old-school casserole recipes that feel like home for boomers and Gen Xers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: This week’s episode is a short one with a single theme. Arielle takes a few minutes to thank the people who keep pressing play, wherever they happen to be spending this Thursday, from a crowded family table to a Friendsgiving far from home. Stay for a friendly note about The Optimist Daily’s push to welcome 100 new Emissaries before the year is out. Arielle and Karissa are back with a full roundup next week. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Arielle: Hi, everyone. It’s Arielle from The Optimist Daily. No full roundup this week. Karissa and I are taking a little breather, but we didn’t want the week to go by without saying hi and saying thank you. In the US, it’s Thanksgiving week. I know a lot of you aren’t in the US and plenty of you might not celebrate it at all. As longtime listeners know, I’m Canadian, and I live in Amsterdam, so this Thursday is a pretty normal day for me, too. But I love the spirit of Thanksgiving, stopping for a moment to notice what’s good in your life and who helped make it that way. And you don’t need a turkey or a long weekend for that. So here’s what we at The Optimist Daily are grateful for this year. You. Every week, we go looking for people fixing things, like the communities restoring rivers, the teenagers creating education programs for their underserved peers locally and globally, and the cities trying something new to make art and books more accessible. Then we get to share those stories with people who want to hear them. That still feels like a gift. Your messages, your emails, the stories you send our way, the fact that you press play, like, follow, and/or subscribe at all, it means a lot to me and Karissa and the rest of our team. I also have one small ask. The Optimist Daily runs on the support of our Emissaries. They’re the readers and listeners who chip in so we can keep doing this without any paywalls and keep good news out there for everyone. Our goal is to welcome one hundred new Emissaries before the end of the year, and we’re just about at the halfway point. If this show has made your week a little lighter or given you something hopeful to bring up at dinner, we’d love for you to be one of those one hundred. As you plan your year-end donations, becoming an Emissary is a lovely way to say thanks back. And with Giving Tuesday coming up next week, we hope you’ll encourage your circle to support The Optimist Daily, too. You can find the link in the show notes. And if that’s not in the cards for you right now, that’s completely okay. Sharing an episode, an article, or a social media post helps at least one more person add something positive to their day, and that little bit of positivity can turn a whole day around. It’s a chain reaction that starts with something so small, and it’s more powerful than it looks. So thank you again for being part of this Optimist movement. However you’re spending this week, whether it’s at a big table full of family, at a Friendsgiving if you’re away from home, curled up for a quiet night in, or if it’s just another Thursday, I hope you get a moment to feel thankful for something. Karissa and I will be back next week with a full roundup. Until then, take care of each other. Bye for now. items.descriptionOriginal: Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Growing up, many of us watched our grandparents prepare for the season by bringing out thick cotton razais , spreading handwoven durries , and opening curtains to let the afternoon sun in. These simple habits can still help us stay comfortable, reduce electricity bills, and make better use of things we already own. Here are eight traditional and sustainable ways to keep your home warmer this winter without constantly relying on a room heater. 1. Make the most of the winter sun Open curtains and shutters in rooms that receive direct sunlight during the day. Let sunlight fall on floors, walls, and furniture. Once evening approaches, draw the curtains to reduce the chill coming through windows. Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Photograph: (Architectural Digest) Thicker curtains can provide an additional layer between the room and cold window panes. This is a humble form of passive solar heating. Traditional homes in our country were often designed around local climates, using natural light, ventilation, and locally available materials. Vernacular architecture in India offers useful examples of how traditional building designs work with natural conditions to create comfortable living spaces. 2. Bring out the traditional razais and quilts A well-filled cotton razai , woollen blanket, or quilt can make a bed comfortable without consuming electricity. Layer a lighter blanket beneath a thicker quilt on particularly cold nights. Keep an additional throw near the sofa for chilly evenings. Instead of replacing bedding every winter, air it on a dry, sunny day and repair loose seams or worn covers. Store it only when completely dry, preferably in a clean cotton bag. Reusing and maintaining bedding helps extend its life and reduces unnecessary purchases. 3. Cover cold floors with durries and rugs Stone and tiled floors can feel particularly cold during winter mornings. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas, such as beside the bed, near the sofa, and in a reading corner. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas. Photograph: (Amazon.in) You do not need to cover the entire floor. A few strategically placed rugs can make everyday spaces more comfortable. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Shake it outdoors regularly and keep it dry to prevent dampness and unpleasant smells. 4. Layer clothing with natural fabrics A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Wear a few layers that can be added or removed as temperatures change. Woollen garments and hand-me-downs can last for several years when cared for properly. If you need something new, consider repairing an old garment or buying a durable piece from a local maker instead of choosing something that may only last one season. 5. Use old fabric to block cold air Cold air can enter through gaps beneath doors and around windows. Instead of buying plastic draught stoppers, repurpose old household textiles. Roll an old towel or stitch leftover cotton fabric into a long cushion and place it beneath doors to limit cold air entering from outside. Check window frames for gaps and use suitable removable sealing strips where necessary. However, avoid blocking ventilation openings, particularly in kitchens and bathrooms, as homes need adequate airflow. 6. Spend more time in one sunny room Rather than trying to keep every room equally warm, arrange your daily activities in the part of the house that receives the most sunlight. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Move a chair, work desk, or floor cushion closer to a sunny spot during the day. Close doors to rooms that are not being used, particularly those that remain noticeably colder. This helps you make better use of naturally available warmth without needing additional appliances. 7. Take inspiration from traditional Himalayan homes Traditional homes in colder parts of the country provide useful lessons in sustainable construction. In Himachal Pradesh, Kath-Kuni houses use alternating layers of stone and timber , with thick walls and mud plaster. Their construction helps insulate interiors and retain warmth. The revival of Kath-Kuni architecture in Himachal Pradesh shows how traditional building techniques and locally available materials can preserve architectural knowledge. Similarly, homes in Ladakh have traditionally used mud, stone, willow, and poplar to respond to the region's harsh winters. Traditional building techniques in Ladakh offer examples of how natural materials can be incorporated into contemporary homes. While these construction techniques cannot directly be replicated in apartments, they demonstrate the importance of choosing materials and designs suited to local climates. 8. Keep your home dry and ventilated Damp rooms can feel colder and may encourage mould growth. Dry wet clothes outdoors when the weather permits, wipe condensation from windows, and use kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans when cooking or bathing. A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Photograph: (Pexels) Open windows briefly when outdoor conditions are suitable to allow fresh air to circulate. Keeping a home warm should not mean sealing it completely. Adequate ventilation is important for maintaining a healthy indoor environment. A warmer home through mindful choices Keeping your home comfortable during winter does not always require expensive appliances or renovations. Traditional architecture also offers lessons in building homes that respond to their surroundings. By combining these practices with mindful consumption, households can stay comfortable while reducing unnecessary energy use. These measures may not replace safe heating during severe cold , but they can reduce the need to rely on room heaters constantly.

items.descriptionOriginal: What if a healthy, protein-rich breakfast took just 30 seconds to prepare? 🚀 Yash Kalra set out to solve a problem he believed millions of Indians were facing: inadequate protein consumption. But his entrepreneurial journey wasn’t easy. After a failed business and with almost no money left, he decided to start again with an idea that could change India’s breakfast habits. That’s how GOAT Life was born — a high-protein, no-added-sugar oatmeal that can be prepared in just 30 seconds. But getting the recipe right took serious work. 🌱 Yash tested over 50 recipes and even took to street sales to understand what customers wanted and perfect his product. And the hard work paid off! Today, GOAT Life reportedly generates ₹31 crore in monthly revenue, with a Shark Tank deal adding another milestone to his entrepreneurial journey. From a failed business to building a fast-growing breakfast brand, Yash’s story is a reminder that sometimes the biggest opportunities come from solving everyday problems. What do you think of a 30-second protein-packed breakfast? items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. City of tomorrow At first glance, the sky seems to be the limit for Utah City, a new community in one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, with the developer citing the cost of constructing high rises as the only constraint. The development checks all the boxes for the kind of sustainable, pedestrian-first urban living we often cover at RTBC: high density, walkability, green spaces, convenient transit options. And the project is ambitious , expected to be finished in 15 to 20 years. But Utah City faces heavy scrutiny, as Grist and the Salt Lake Tribune report in a story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. Though one new resident describes it as “rad” and “vibey,” members of the local city council call it a “gamble,” expressing skepticism that such a community makes sense in a place full of freeways and single-family homes. As one council member put it: “Walkability I don’t care about. [It] forces a lifestyle the average person isn’t living. Most people drive a car.” Becca says: If you build it, will they come? This is a fascinating look at a dense, transit-centered development that seems great on paper but may not be compatible with local desires. Popularity contest Imagine the U.S. without red states or blue states, just millions of people whose votes all matter equally. That’s what would happen if we got rid of the Electoral College, and according to a New York Times opinion piece shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, thanks to this month’s election, this idea is closer than ever to becoming a reality. Now that Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin will have Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in their legislatures, those states may sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. As its name suggests, the compact would make it so that presidential elections are decided by the popular vote. Eighteen states have already adopted it, and if these five sign, writes Jesse Wegman, senior fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice, “then as early as November 2028 we could experience something no one has ever seen — a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.” Will says: I’d been half-listening to the news about states abandoning the Electoral College, but I hadn’t fully absorbed how profoundly this could impact American democracy — in a good way — until I read this piece . What else we’re reading Himalayan Communities Are Relying on Centuries-Old Water Solutions In the Face of Climate Change — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Time Goats vs. vines: Baby goats devour invasive plants, save native trees in Mecklenburg County — shared by Will Doig from WFAE NYC Citi Bike member rides to be capped at $3.65 after Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft — shared by Rebecca Worby from Gothamist From our readers… Earlier this year, we published a story about wild European bison returning to the Carpathian Mountains of southwestern Romania. This week, we heard from Alex at Live Species , a small independent site that shows the latest published count for each of the world’s rarest wild animals, and those, like bison, whose numbers have recovered enough to tick up past 1,000. “The bison page shows none living free in 1927 and 9,762 in free-living herds in December 2024, a head count from the European Bison Pedigree Book,” writes Alex. “The page also credits WWF-Romania and Rewilding Europe for moving bison into the Țarcu Mountains, where they now range free.” Thanks, Alex! The post What We’re Reading: Building a Walkable City From Scratch appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Last week, on 19th November, 2026, a video started doing the rounds on social media. You may have seen it. A woman is standing in a park in Mumbai, crying. Around her, workers are cutting down trees. One of them is a big old banyan. The workers say it is about 35 years old. She shakes her head — it has been here much longer than that, she says. "This is our tree. This is not their tree to cut." The woman is Pooja Ruparel. If you have watched Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge , you will remember her as the little girl in the film. The park is Nana-Nani Park in Versova. On 18 November, Mumbai's civic body, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), started cutting trees there to make room for part of a new coastal road. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pooja Ruparel (@poojaruparel) Pooja shared the clips on Instagram. Before long, news websites were writing about them. Actors like Dia Mirza and Richa Chadha spoke up too. People have not stopped talking about it since. Not everyone sees it the same way. Some people felt her pain. Others asked: what will crying change? Doesn't a crowded city like Mumbai need new roads? Pooja says the tree was protected and cutting it was illegal. The BMC says it had every permission it needed. But set the arguments aside for a moment, and the video leaves you with a few simple questions. What do we really lose when a tree that has grown for 25 years is cut down? Can't we just dig it up and plant it somewhere else? And does building a road always have to mean losing a park? Scientists have actually tried to answer the first question. It takes roughly 400 saplings to do the work of one old tree. That is the estimate of Andreas Roloff, a forestry scientist at TU Dresden in Germany. To match the shade, cooling, air filtration and carbon storage of a single mature tree with a 20-metre crown, he calculated, a city would need to plant around 400 young ones. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich arrived at a similar conclusion from another direction: when an old city tree is replaced with a young one, the tree count stays the same, but often more than 90 per cent of its benefits disappear. India has tried to put a number on it, too. In 2021, an expert committee appointed by the Supreme Court valued a tree at ₹74,500 for every year it lives — counting the oxygen, biofertiliser, compost and micronutrients it gives away free — and observed that an old tree and a fresh sapling are simply not equivalent. Those figures have been tested on the ground in Mumbai this past week. Despite of many efforts by our community members to save Nana Nani Park, the trees there are being cut. Mumbai already lacks third places for people to hangout, Mumbai's Air is unbreathable. Yet they want to make it worse! There seems no end to this destruction! https://t.co/61pIJNHNmw — Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 18, 2026 On 18 November 2026, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) began felling trees at Nana-Nani Park in Versova to make way for an interchange on the Coastal Road North (Versova–Bhayandar) project. Under the approved plan, 184 trees in the park are to be cut and another 164 transplanted to Seven Bungalows nearby. Around 44 were reportedly brought down on the first day. The park was built in 2001 on what had been a dumping ground. Residents planted and tended its trees for 25 years; many of them have spoken of raising those trees like children. Videos of the felling — including the loss of an old banyan — spread quickly, and protests followed. More than 3,200 objections had been filed with the civic body earlier in the year, and residents had proposed an alternative alignment. The BMC maintains that all permissions were obtained and that the felling and compensatory plantation plans were cleared by its Tree Authority. There is one more detail worth knowing. Under Maharashtra's 2021 amendment to its urban tree law, only trees estimated to be 50 years or older are classified as "heritage trees" and given special protection. Most of Nana-Nani Park's trees, at around 25, fall well short of that line. Swami Prem Parivartan thinks the line is drawn in the wrong place. Better known as Peepal Baba, and often called India's Tree Father, he planted his first sapling in 1977, at the age of 11, at the urging of a schoolteacher. Nearly five decades later, he and his Give Me Trees Trust have planted and preserved more than 2.5 crore trees across over 200 districts in India. He spoke to The Better India about what Mumbai stands to lose — and what it could still choose to do differently. 'Any tree older than 20 years should be a protected living form' Nana-Nani Park is losing 184 established trees, most of them mature. Ecologically, what does it mean for one neighbourhood to lose that many trees at once? "Any tree that is more than 20 years old should, I believe, be recognised as a protected entity. It should be considered a protected living form. Nana-Nani Park is not an isolated case. Similar disputes have surfaced in Nashik, around Bhimashankar, in Uttarakhand and across north India. Photograph: (Instagram/@navneetmishraa) "There are so many ecosystem services associated with a tree. This is not just about timber. Trees provide shelter and shade, help with carbon sequestration, and support pollinators such as bees, birds and butterflies. They provide nesting and roosting spaces, retain moisture, prevent soil erosion and support the microbial populations that live around their roots. They also help create microclimates wherever they grow." In other words, a neighbourhood that loses 184 trees does not lose 184 objects. It loses 184 small systems — each one sheltering, cooling, feeding and holding soil in place for everything around it. 'You cannot protect yourselves if you destroy the elders of the natural world' In a city as dense as Mumbai, surrounded by concrete, roads and buildings, how important are mature trees? And what happens to the birds and insects that have built their lives around them? For Peepal Baba, a tree that has stood for two or three decades has become part of the community's living fabric. Birds roost in it, insects feed on it, and a web of soil microbes depends on its roots. Remove it, he says, and those relationships do not simply relocate. "Trees are a very important part of biodiversity. You cannot preserve your culture, or even protect yourselves, if you keep cutting down, chopping up, eliminating and destroying the elders of the natural world — while thinking that compensatory afforestation will somehow make up for it." The science on heat backs the urgency. A recent study from Northwestern University tracking Chicago's tree canopy found that the near-term health benefits of tree cover come largely from big trees already standing, and that protecting existing canopy may do more good than planting alone. A sapling planted today will take decades to cast the shade that a 25-year-old tree casts now. Nana-Nani Park's trees were planted by people who are now grandparents themselves. They watched the saplings grow into a canopy over 25 years. Photograph: (Instagram/@navneetmishraa) It is also why he is uneasy with replanting that happens far away. For the Coastal Road North project as a whole, the BMC's compensatory plantation of more than 19,500 trees is planned in Panvel, citing a lack of space within Mumbai. His view is simple: "If trees are cut down somewhere, the same species should be planted as close as possible to the location where they were removed." The work you don't see in a park When we look at a city park, we usually see trees and benches. What less visible ecological processes are going on inside an established green space? Much of what an old tree does happens out of sight, Peepal Baba explains — in the soil around its roots, in the moisture it holds, and in the cooler pocket of air beneath its canopy. These are the processes that take years to establish and cannot be planted overnight. "Wherever a tree grows, it creates a microclimate. It retains moisture. Its roots hold the soil together and support an entire microbial population. Bees, birds and butterflies come to it. So many forms of life depend on one tree." That matters in a city built on reclaimed land and battered by monsoon flooding and rising heat. Shade lowers surface temperatures. Roots slow run-off. Canopy catches rain before it hits the ground. In Nana-Nani Park, all of this was being done quietly, for free, by trees that residents had planted on a former garbage dump. 'Transplanting sounds wonderful. In most cases, the tree does not survive.' Under the plan, 164 trees will be transplanted. Residents had also suggested relocating mature trees rather than felling them. Is transplantation a real alternative? This is where Peepal Baba is most emphatic. "There is something people find very appealing to hear: that a tree has been uprooted from one place and planted somewhere else. It sounds like a wonderful solution. But scientifically, the success rate is extremely low." He points out that countries such as Japan, Germany, Switzerland, Italy and France have had better results — but with different climates, better technology and, crucially, years of committed aftercare. "In India, when a tree is uprooted and moved to another location, nobody even goes back to check on it. Nobody ensures that it is watered. Even if you instruct a contractor to move a tree, once the two- or three-month tender period ends, the contractor will not return to maintain it. They will not make sure it gets water or manure, or that it is protected from cows, buffaloes, goats, nilgai — and human beings. In most cases, the tree simply does not survive." Mumbai's own records suggest he has reason to be sceptical. In 2020, the city's municipal commissioner admitted before the Bombay High Court that only about 36 per cent of trees transplanted for the Metro III line had survived after two years. A later RTI analysis by the Watchdog Foundation found that of 6,043 trees transplanted across the city's wards, 4,444 had died. Mumbaikars are speaking, are you listening. Today at Nana Nani Park people gathered to demand that @mybmc stop the cutting and where the 48 trees will be transplanted, if it will be an actual transplantation, not sapling-tokenism and independently review the alternative before causing irreversible damage. #savenanananipark — Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 21, 2026 Which is why, he says, the debate should shift altogether: "At least in our country, uprooting a tree and planting it somewhere else should not even be considered a viable argument . The discussion should be about protecting the trees that already exist." If removal is truly unavoidable, he says, the replacement should be the same species, planted as close as possible, at the greatest height and maturity possible, with the largest root ball. And if anything must be moved, it should be the young. "If it is a relatively new plantation — trees that are two, three, four or five years old — then perhaps those can be removed. That may still be manageable. But a large, old tree simply cannot adjust to being uprooted." 'Trees are not anti-development' Nana-Nani Park has become shorthand for infrastructure versus ecology. How do you see that debate? Peepal Baba rejects the framing entirely. "The debate should not be about infrastructure versus ecology, or infrastructure versus old trees. If you want to build infrastructure, you must also acknowledge the life-giving features of the natural world, and the enormous role trees play in it. "Trees are not anti-development. They are not anti-infrastructure. Build your infrastructure, by all means. But do it with a little sensitivity, compassion and empathy. Please do not touch the old trees." He argues the two are not just compatible but dependent on each other — and that the market already knows it. "The beauty and value of a landscape , including its real estate value, rises when there are beautiful trees around, when there is water, when there are flowers, and when birds, bees and butterflies are present. Both can coexist. In fact, they are interdependent." Nana-Nani Park is not an isolated case. Similar disputes have surfaced in Nashik, around Bhimashankar, in Uttarakhand and across north India. Each time, he says, the same question returns: was every alternative examined before the oldest trees were marked? The grandparents in the village When asked why an old tree can't simply start over somewhere new, Peepal Baba reaches for an image anyone can recognise. "It is like saying we should uproot our grandparents, or our parents, who have spent their entire lives in one village. Their culture, their habits, their society, their friends and relatives — all of it is rooted in that one place. You cannot simply move them and settle them in another village. That is not how life works. They would die a slow death. "The same thing happens to trees." Nana-Nani Park's trees were planted by people who are now grandparents themselves. They watched the saplings grow into a canopy over 25 years. Whatever is built in their place, the residents of Versova will be waiting a long time for that shade to return. "Trees are citizens of our planet, our country, our city, our landscape," Peepal Baba says. "We need to recognise that." Sources: 'One old tree is worth 400 saplings – Dresden forestry expert Andreas Roloff calls for more respect for trees' : By Dresden University of Technology, Published on 25 April 2023 'As urban tree shade shrinks, mortality rises-New study finds that protecting mature trees could help save lives' : By Amanda Morris, Published on 5 August 2026 'BMC's Urban Forest: Miyawaki Trees In Mumbai Face Grim Fate' : By RUCHA KANOLKAR, Published on 22 March 2024

items.descriptionOriginal: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News California Ecohome Wins First Place With a Water-Smart Approach to Landscaping Reading Time: 3 minutes The Arcadia Ecohome Microforest earned top honors in a 2026 landscape contest by combining rainwater and graywater harvesting, drip irrigation, rain gardens, and rewilding practices. In our previous story, we explored how conservation can become something people practice where they live. At the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest in California, that idea extends to one of our most important natural resources: water. This July, the Ecohome was awarded first place in the Upper San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District’s (Upper Water) 2026 Home Landscape Contest as part of Smart Irrigation Month. Smart Irrigation Month is a global campaign the Irrigation Association launched in 2005 to educate homeowners, businesses, growers, and communities about the social, economic, and environmental benefits of water-efficient irrigation. Observed every July, it promotes water efficiency during the peak of summer demand. As backyard growers and homeowners based at the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest, we have supported and participated in the campaign since 2010. Taking part in Smart Irrigation Month 2026 was part of our plan, so we entered Upper Water’s Home Landscape Contest and submitted photos showing how we use smart irrigation practices. On July 31, we learned that the Arcadia Ecohome won first place. Upper Water said the submission demonstrated “thoughtful smart irrigation practices and a strong commitment to water conservation.” The prize was a Smart Flow Monitor Device. For me, the recognition also reflects something I have learned through years of participating in Smart Irrigation Month. A “smart” irrigation system is not a one-size-fits-all solution. It combines and integrates different applications to use available water resources more effectively. We have applied that approach across the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest, where more than 500 trees, shrubs, and vines grow on a half-acre residential lot. The landscape is also a Certified Wildlife Habitat, Certified Pollinator Habitat, and Certified Monarch Waystation. Our water-smart system combines hand watering, deep watering, drip irrigation, rainwater and graywater harvesting, permeable surfaces, forest-floor covering, and distributed rain-garden subsystems. One example is at the main irrigation station serving the rear yard. Alongside a hose bibb and the automatic drip irrigation control station is a repurposed DIY water barrel that collects rainwater from a downspout. Graywater from the Energy Star-rated washing machine in the nearby laundry room and from sinks and tubs in the upstairs main bathroom is also incorporated into the system. These different water sources are integrated into a small rain garden. Drip irrigation pipes run beneath an organic mulch layer of fallen leaves, twigs, and brush around the tree roots. Through “leave-the-leaves” and rewilding practices, we keep organic material on site rather than removing it as waste. The forest-floor layer retains moisture and supports soil biodiversity, while the mulch also helps minimize evaporation from the irrigation system. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, helping plants receive moisture efficiently while reducing unnecessary water use. Photo by Nebular on Unsplash. Water is managed in other parts of the property through a distributed rain-garden system integrated with the irrigation subsystems. One section includes a rainwater harvesting system with a downspout, a DIY water barrel, and a rain garden with both manual and automatic irrigation lines. Rocks and gravel create a flow channel that carries overflow from the rain barrel into the garden. The goal is not simply to water plants. It is to make use of different water resources while supporting a landscape that functions as habitat. That approach has also allowed the Ecohome to educate the community. Because the property adjoins Camino Grove and Camino Grove Park and receives considerable foot traffic, I installed educational signage in the front yard to raise public awareness of the landscape’s features. The top of the sign features an “Ocean Friendly Garden” designation awarded by the Surfrider Foundation for conservation, permeability, stormwater retention, and reduced urban runoff pollution in water bodies. The Ecohome has also hosted voluntary educational workshops and tours and supported awareness campaigns, including World Water Week, World Water Day, World Water Monitoring Day, Fix-A-Leak Week, and Smart Irrigation Month. In June 2012, our community partner, the Chinese American Construction Professionals (CACP), joined us for a grassroots workshop and tour at the Ecohome in support of Smart Irrigation Month. More recently, a workshop and tour on July 26, 2025, brought together guests, volunteers, and news reporters in the Ecohome’s permeable front yard. The event was later featured by the Epoch Times and SingTao Daily. The first-place award from Upper Water is meaningful because it recognizes an approach we have been developing at the Ecohome for years. More importantly, it gives us another opportunity to show that water conservation doesn’t have to be separate from habitat creation, rewilding, or community education. A residential landscape can capture rainwater, reuse graywater, reduce evaporation, manage stormwater, support wildlife, and give people a place to learn. For me, that is what makes an irrigation system truly smart: not one solution working alone, but different practices working together to make better use of the water and resources already around us. The post California Ecohome Wins First Place With a Water-Smart Approach to Landscaping appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Floating Wetlands Cut Wastewater Emissions in Australian Treatment Lagoons Reading Time: 3 minutes A world-first trial in Australia found that floating wetlands made of native reeds cut greenhouse gas emissions from a wastewater lagoon by up to 36%. Floating wetlands built from native reeds and sedges have cut greenhouse gas emissions from a wastewater lagoon by more than a quarter. A two-year trial on Phillip Island in southeastern Australia tracked the results continuously using solar-powered sensors. Researchers call it the first real-world test at full operational scale. RMIT University led the trial with Westernport Water, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, and Deakin University. Wastewater treatment already accounts for about 1.6 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. That share is expected to grow as more countries improve access to sanitation. Scientists floated a platform of native plants roughly the size of one and a half tennis courts on part of a treatment lagoon. Plant roots dangled directly into the water below. A second, untreated section of the same lagoon served as a comparison point throughout the study. The lagoon itself held roughly 14 million liters of wastewater at the Westernport Water treatment site. High nutrient levels in wastewater create ideal conditions for the microbes that generate greenhouse gases in the first place. Floating wetlands aim to interrupt that cycle by giving plants and their root microbes a foothold directly on the water’s surface. Carbon dioxide emissions from the floating wetland section dropped by up to 36% compared to the untreated lagoon. Methane fell by up to 66%, and nitrous oxide emissions fell by up to 18%. Combined, overall greenhouse gas emissions fell by roughly 31%. Researchers expected floating wetlands to help mainly by removing nutrients from the water over time. Instead, emissions began dropping within four to seven months, well before nutrient levels changed much. That gap surprised the research team and remains only partly understood. Scientists suspect the roots host microbial communities that interact with the gases in ways we still don’t fully understand. Testing those interactions directly will take further research. For now, the emissions drop stands as a real-world result even without a confirmed explanation; one researcher plans to keep investigating as the technology moves toward wider use. Some treatment plants already use floating wetlands to soak up excess nitrogen and phosphorus before discharging or reusing water. This trial adds emissions reduction to that established role. The approach requires no major new infrastructure, since existing lagoons can be retrofitted directly. Floating wetlands now tackle greenhouse gas emissions alongside their established role in removing nitrogen and phosphorus from wastewater, with existing treatment lagoons retrofitted directly and no major new infrastructure required. Photo courtesy of ScienceDirect . Some practical details still need attention before wider rollout. Trimming the plants keeps them healthy and boosts nutrient uptake, but cutting also triggers short bursts of methane release. Researchers are working out how to manage that trade-off without losing the overall benefit. The trial produced nearly one metric ton of harvested plant material over its run. Turning that material into biochar could lock its carbon away for the long term. Without that step, some of the climate benefits could eventually be undone. Building on these results, researchers are now testing floating wetlands on farm dams in Victoria’s Bass Coast region. According to the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, Australia has roughly 1.8 million farm dams that could potentially benefit from the same approach. Farm dams often receive heavy loads of nutrients and organic matter from livestock, which can drive their own emissions. Water utilities worldwide have few affordable options for cutting emissions from open-air lagoons today. Most existing fixes involve covering ponds or installing mechanical treatment systems, both of which are expensive. A planted, low-maintenance platform offers a much cheaper starting point for utilities on tight budgets. If floating wetlands prove effective across different water bodies, they could offer a low-tech tool for cutting emissions at a global scale. The approach works with existing infrastructure rather than requiring costly rebuilds. For a sector still searching for affordable climate solutions, that combination of simplicity and results may be exactly what’s needed. The post Floating Wetlands Cut Wastewater Emissions in Australian Treatment Lagoons appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Your weight has been creeping up. You still feel absolutely fine. So is there really anything to worry about? Feeling fine doesn’t always tell you what’s happening inside. Extra weight can increase the work your heart and blood vessels have to do, and that can contribute to a higher risk of high blood pressure, which can be present without obvious symptoms. So don’t look at just one number. Look at the trend. Is your weight gradually increasing? Is your waist changing too? A weight or waist trend is a reason to check, not a diagnosis. Start with changes you can sustain: balanced meals, regular movement, strength exercises and adequate sleep. Then speak with a qualified doctor about what a realistic weight-management plan could look like for you. Because seeking help with your weight is preventive care. Not judgement. Not failure. Not cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your metabolic health. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #BloodPressure #WeightManagement #PreventiveCare #MetabolicHealth [weight gain and high blood pressure, can weight affect blood pressure, high blood pressure without symptoms, weight management and heart health, India]

Ο προφορικός ιστορικός Ε…
items.descriptionOriginal: When a writer moved to a small Vermont town and began helping elders record their life stories, what emerged was far more than local history -- it was evidence of something science now confirms: that storytelling is, at its core, a biological act of human bonding, one that physically synchronizes the brains of speaker and listener. Oral historian Esther Ehrlich found herself falling in love with every single person she interviewed -- even the medical malpractice insurance executive she'd initially dreaded meeting. She notes that "oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood." Holocaust survivor Helen Marks has watched thousands of students be moved in ways no textbook could achieve, and hospice volunteer Neal Allen discovered that helping the dying retrieve long-buried memories wasn't sorrowful work but "quite extraordinary." What sharing stories quietly insists is that every life, told honestly, becomes a gift -- not only to those who receive it, but to the person finally brave enough to offer it.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Fly Larvae to Soup Kitchens: Local Ideas for Reducing Food Loss and Waste Globally Reading Time: 3 minutes Schools in Nairobi, soup kitchens in Lima, and market vendors in Quezon City show what works in reducing food loss and waste globally. Reducing food loss and waste globally is one of the most direct ways to feed people and cut emissions. About 13% of food is lost between harvest and retail. Another 19% of the food that reaches consumers is wasted in shops, restaurants, and homes. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) put a number on that waste in its 2024 Food Waste Index. In 2022, the world threw away about 1.05 billion tonnes of food, or roughly one billion meals a day. That same year, 783 million people went hungry. Households wasted the most, about 631 million tonnes. The average person wasted 79 kilograms of food that year, about the weight of an adult. Wasted food also harms the climate. Food loss and waste produce up to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from aviation. The United Nations marks the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste every September 29. The 2026 theme focused on the transformative potential of cutting both. For CGIAR, a global network of agricultural research centers, the day was a chance to rethink the problem. Dr. Mukani Moyo leads urban food systems research in CGIAR’s Food Frontiers and Security Program. She argues that losses often begin on farms, long before food reaches a city. In her view, cities cannot tackle waste without looking upstream. Perishable crops show why. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) lists fruits, vegetables, roots, and tubers among the foods most at risk. For example, rough handling, poor storage, and weak market links often cause potatoes and sweet potatoes to be lost. The fixes are practical. Better-adapted crop varieties, improved storage, and local processing all help. Solar-powered cold storage can keep produce fresh in places with little electricity. In Nairobi, schoolchildren are tackling the problem from the other end of the chain. At three schools and a farmers’ hub, they feed lunch leftovers and kitchen scraps to black soldier fly larvae. Raised in containers called biopods, the larvae eat organic waste quickly and grow rich in protein. The World Vegetable Center and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture lead the project. Each biopod started in mid-2026 with 3 kilograms of young larvae. The first harvests at the schools weighed 15 to 19 kilograms each. In the second cycle, larvae production rose by 30 to 60%. Farmers feed the larvae to pigs and poultry, and one farmer reports her pigs compete eagerly for them. The leftover material, called frass, goes back to school gardens as fertilizer. Black soldier fly larvae turn lunch scraps into animal feed, a small step toward reducing food loss and waste globally. Photo by Rodrick rajive lal on Wikimedia Commons This matters in Africa, where up to 40% of food is lost or wasted along informal urban supply chains. Projects like this show how reducing food loss and waste globally can start in a single schoolyard. Lima, Peru, takes a different approach. Community food rescue groups collect surplus food from local producers. They pass it on to ollas comunes, community soup kitchens that feed families in low-income neighborhoods. Researchers from the International Potato Center have studied these kitchens as a source of community resilience. Food that might have spoiled instead becomes nutritious meals. Vietnamese farmers are closing the loop on their own land. They compost livestock manure and crop leftovers, returning the nutrients to their fields. That cuts waste and reduces the need to buy fertilizer. Ghanaian researchers are studying how to turn large volumes of city food waste back into farm inputs. The goal is to scale promising local solutions beyond small pilots. In Quezon City, Philippines, the Vendor Business School trains vegetable vendors in safe food handling and business skills. It also teaches them to cope with heat that spoils produce. The program started in 2024 with 140 vendors. City leaders saw enough value to make it permanent. A 2025 city ordinance now writes the Vendor Business School into local law. Vendors report more confidence and more repeat customers. Japan has cut its food waste by 18%, and the United Kingdom by 31%. Both offer models for reducing food loss and waste globally. The UN aims to halve food waste by 2030. Moyo stresses that technology alone will not succeed in reducing food loss and waste globally. Scaling up requires finance, infrastructure, skills, and better research on where and why food is lost. It also requires farmers, traders, businesses, and city governments to work together. Local context matters most. A solution that works in Nairobi may need changes before it works in Accra or Lima. Reducing food loss and waste globally will depend on many local answers, each fitted to its place. The post From Fly Larvae to Soup Kitchens: Local Ideas for Reducing Food Loss and Waste Globally appeared first on Happy Eco News .
