items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone. The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 , passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law. How the abortion pardons work Records deleted, or treated as deleted The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased. Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls , said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said. What remains illegal The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges. Ending a Victorian law’s reach Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along. Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said. It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was. Reactions to the pardons Providers and advocates Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said. Opponents of decriminalization Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.” For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: An evocative shot of a waterfall of fog spilling into the sea in Mallorca, Spain, took the top honor in the Royal Meteorological Society’s 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition. Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the image during dawn’s first light, the rising sun illuminating the mist. “There’s a fabulous sense of flow in this image,” competition judge Angela Nicholson said in a statement. “The clouds are transformed into a river flowing over the cliffs. Francisco’s choice of exposure has captured the movement of the clouds perfectly below a beautiful sky with subtle color transitions.” Now in its second decade, the competition highlights the beauty and power of weather while raising awareness of the environmental issues that threaten life on Earth — things like heat, fires, and floods. Thirty images were shortlisted from a pool of over 5,500 taken in 13 countries. In addition to Rodríguez’s shot, eight photos were recognized as winners or runners-up across four categories: public vote, mobile, climate, and main. “These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, per SWNS, adding: “Crucially, many of these images also deliver a powerful and urgent message about the global impact of climate change on environments ranging from parched agricultural land to melting ice caps.” The annual competition is free to enter and open to photographers of all ages and abilities, with judges looking for images that combine skill, meteorological observation, and storytelling. Take a look at the other winners and runners-up, with captions courtesy of contest organizers. Public Vote | Winner “Misty Sunrise Over the Long Coc Tea Hills” by Mahmudul Hasan Mahmudul Hasan/RMetS/SWNS “Captured in the delicate light of dawn, this breathtaking photo reveals the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.” Mobile Category | Winner “A Winter Morning” by Aung Soe Min Aung Soe MinRMetS/SWNS “A calm winter morning reveals Kuthodaw Pagoda rising through the mist and fog. Aung Soe Min captured the sun rays filtering across the landscape, creating a beautiful sunrise that captures the warmth of the weather and the peaceful serenity of this sacred site in Myanmar.” Climate Award | Winner “Fire” by Erfan Samanfar Erfan Samanfar/RMetS/SWNS “From Marvdasht, Iran, in October 2025, Erfan Samanfar captured a striking image of a farmer attempting to protect their land as fire spreads across the landscape.” Main Category | Runner-Up “Sunrise and Morning Glow” by Weilu Chen Weilu ChenRMetS/SWNS “As the sun rose over the Hong Kong Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the morning sky was transformed into a spectacular display of golden light.” Public Vote | Runner-Up “Triple Strike NYC” by Dan Martland Dan Martland/RMetS/SWNS “Talk about being in the right place at the right time. From Bayonne, New Jersey, Dan Martland captured this spectacular scene overlooking the New York City skyline, as three lightning strikes lit the sky above the city.” Mobile Category | Runner-Up “A Rainbow Over Loch Duck” by Anthony Bird Anthony BirdRMetS/SWNS “Framed by the rolling hills and water below, a magnificent rainbow arches across the landscape of Loch Duck, Scotland. The scene caught Anthony Bird’s eye so quickly that there was barely time to think, as he simply had to ‘run outside the Airbnb’ to capture it.” Climate Award | Runner-Up “Castles in the Wind” by Andres Miraglia Andres Miraglia/RMetS/SWNS “As an iceberg drifted away from the glacier that released it in Antarctica’s Paradise Harbour, Andres Miraglia captured the moment against a pristine sunset.” Main Category | Third Place “A Supercell in the Sandhills of Nebraska” by Laura Hedien Laura Hedien/RMetS/SWNS “While out storm chasing in the Nebraska sandhills, ‘Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night,’ explains Laura Hedien.” This article was originally written by Dean Murray for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets .

items.descriptionOriginal: A family in Los Angeles’ Lake Balboa neighborhood has a holiday tradition that dates back about 80 years. Every Thanksgiving, the host and a helper write “Turkey Notes” for all the loved ones attending the feast. The only rule? Include the word “turkey” somewhere in the text. The notes range from silly rhymes (“Turkey red, turkey yellow, turkey says you’re an awesome fellow”) to sincere celebrations of guests’ recent accomplishments. The writers then wrap the notes in colorful tissue paper and “roll them like a Tootsie Roll with ribbon on each end,” Nice News reader Sadie shared, adding that the ritual makes for some of her favorite memories. Sadie is one of the dozens of readers who answered our call earlier this month to submit the seasonal family traditions they partake in. Multiple made us laugh out loud, while others were deeply touching. We rounded up a selection for you to peruse — and they just might inspire new shared activities for your own holiday gatherings. Iuliia Anisimova—iStock/Getty Images Plus The hood ornament from my husband’s mother’s car he wrecked as a teenager. It was his only Christmas gift that year. It’s the first ornament we hang every year. – Katherine (Lake Wylie, South Carolina) Thanksgiving Eve, we have a family/friend gathering called BAGG, which stands for Bucket-A-Go-Go. We started this tradition because my husband was tired of eating turkey on Thanksgiving and wanted a change. Nobody wanted to change the Thanksgiving menu, so BAGG was created! Every family brings their own meal but the No. 1 rule is that it must NOT be turkey! The tradition started with a bucket of chicken but now it is whatever the family brings (but NO turkey). One year someone brought a turkey sandwich and they were booed! – Lauren (Roanoke, Virginia) Cookies! We have a cookie trade! Everyone bakes two to three different types of cookies and then we get together for a Christmas party and eat cookies while spending time together. At the end of the get-together, we all split up the cookies so everyone gets to take home a few of each type of cookie. – Stacy (La Mesa, California) My three children were young when their dad and I divorced. He lived in a different state and this meant the children were always torn between celebrating Thanksgiving and Christmas with either mom or dad. So the children and I invited our exclusive holiday — Thanksmas — which was celebrated in early December. We decorated with both fall and Christmas decorations, cooked a meal of Thanksgiving and Christmas dishes, and enjoyed holiday music. And they never had to decide between celebrating Thanksmas with mom or dad each year — it was ours, and ours alone! – Norine (Winchester, Virginia) In our family, we write funny clues on the gifts. While opening them, we read the clues aloud and try to guess what the gift is. – Jennifer (Duluth, Minnesota) My brother sent me an orange tree the year our dad died. Purple and orange were his favorite colors, so I decorated it with purple ornaments. It now goes up in October and transitions from a Halloween tree with bats to a Thanksgiving tree with turkey hands made by my 10 grandchildren, and then to the Christmas tree. Reminders of both my dad and my thoughtful brother. – Debra (Olathe, Kansas) I love putting out my holiday decorations from my favorite holidays, Diwali and Thanksgiving to Christmas. I also celebrate my decorations every year inside my house trying new styles as I desire after talking with my household for what we all like most. – Sautam (Massachusetts) Every year my husband and I host “Nacho Christmas.” It came about because we both wanted a chill holiday with plenty of quality time with any friends and family that want to stop through. We set up the nacho bar so people can eat whenever they come by — no need to coordinate a meal at a set time. … It’s such a huge hit that a friend had a terrible nightmare where I told her she can’t come anymore and she woke up crying. Nacho Christmas for the win. – Wendy (Chicago, Illinois) My son and I watch a holiday movie every night, beginning with Miracle on 34th Street on Thanksgiving Eve. We will have the tree up and lit as well, and then add a few ornaments every day. We always save a few so friends and family can hang something when they come over. Of course we go to see the tree at Rockefeller Center and the Rockettes every year as well! – Peggy (New York City) Making Aebleskivers, a Danish round ball pancake, on Christmas morning. They are the size of a golf ball and you make them in a pan with round holes. When the bottom of the pancake is cooked, you turn it over to cook the top side using a knitting needle. When done they can be eaten as is or with powdered sugar or honey, or you can split them open and add jam, whipped cream, or pudding in the middle. It has been a family tradition for 100 years. – Kathy (Texas) Butterscotch Schnapps milkshakes. Ice cream, milk, and Schnapps. That’s it. Sit around, talk, and drink. It’s fantastic. – Emery (Saskatchewan, Canada) My family (me, my husband Tim, and our two sons: TJ, 22, and Joey, 18) saves all the holiday cards we receive throughout the season and open them all at once after dessert on Christmas Eve. We started this tradition about 10 years ago and it’s been a favorite of everyone’s. This way, Tim and I can share who our nonlocal friends are, but over time, our sons know them and recognize them, even if they’ve never met them in person. And it’s a good way for someone not to miss some important updates. We just wish more friends and families still sent out cards. We love them. – Amy (Poulsbo, Washington) Every year for Hanukkah when my kids were still at home, we made latkes, played games, lit candles, and invited friends over. Some years, instead of giving individual gifts, we did one big family experience together. When the kids were in their teens, we decided that the first of the eight nights would be dedicated to charity, so instead of exchanging presents, we bought them for others in need or made a donation. – Elaine (Baltimore, Maryland) While raising our children in New Hampshire, we had many winter days where we lost electricity because of ice/snow storms. When the kids were very young, we lost electricity one Christmas Eve. But having a wood stove as the primary way to heat the house, at least we were warm. So, for lighting, we placed lit candles in every room and cooked some basic foods on top of the wood stove. It was magical for the children. This started a tradition on every Christmas Eve of turning off all the lights in the house, lighting only candles, and eating just hors d’oeuvres — which we have now done for 30-plus years. – Jim (North Carolina) Every Christmas, I plan a solo trip that I look forward to all year. I try to fly on Christmas Day and bring a little gift (usually a box of chocolates) for the flight attendants. While flying on the holiday tends to be a little less expensive, the real benefit is that people are kinder and more patient with one another. It reminds me of the airport scene at the beginning of Love Actually . – Marie (Frankfurt) My father is a Methodist minister. When he was in seminary shortly after World War II, he attended a Christmas party. A warm punch was served and he really liked it. He obtained the recipe and we’ve made the wassail punch every year since! We still have the original typed recipe on crinkly typewriter paper. – Carol (Alameda, California) Fruitcakes. Every Halloween weekend, I make fruitcakes with raisins, currants, apricots, pecans, cinnamon, clove, mace, and, yes, some of the traditional citron but less. Sherry and brandy poured over them every weekend until the weeks between Thanksgiving and Christmas. My paternal grandmother kept them in her pantry and I loved to watch her take them out, unwrap the wax paper, and pour sherry through cheesecloth then re-wrap and set on the self. She is with me all the time I make these. – Susan Conklin (Hood River, Oregon) My two sons are grown now, but when they were small they would make an ornament for the tree. The early ones were simple, a scrap of fabric (I had to sew the seams as they were only 2 and 4 years old), stuffed little pillows with fluffy cotton. As the years went by, the ornaments became quite amazing for little hands. As a 4-year-old, my youngest was able to complete a framed cross stitch on his own. This was a tradition until they each left for college. I now hang about 30 wildly creative ornaments on my own tree. – Ki’ihele (Hawai’i) Making gifts for my family and my friends, be it knitted mittens, a painting, or special desserts, while I enjoy the winter scenery outside my kitchen window. – Dianne (River Falls, Wisconsin) About a decade ago, I began a tradition with my son (now 13) that we call the thankful tree. I found a little decorative tree and we have leaf-shaped papers with string. Every night of November, we each write down something we are grateful for from that day, share them out loud, and hang them on the tree. By the end of the month, our tree (and hearts) are bursting with gratitude, and I save and label the “leaves” from each year, so we can look back on memories and gratitude. – Sarah (Denver, Colorado) I am one of 10 children. When we were born, my mother knit us a Christmas stocking with our names on it. As we married and had children, she knit stockings for our spouses and her grandchildren. My brother-in-law built a faux fireplace that we keep at the Elks Club. We get together every Christmas Eve and hang our stockings! There are usually 40-50 stockings! – Mary (Warren, New Jersey) Every December, we delight in attending a carol service at a huge old church on Bloor St. — a main street in the downtown. People put twenties on the collection plate which goes entirely to support the Toronto Star Santa Claus Fund begun by newspaper editor Joe Atkinson so underprivileged children would receive a Christmas gift. Boxes contain mitts, warm hats, books, candy, etc. This was especially welcomed during the Great Depression and continues the spirit of giving to this day! – Gail (Toronto, Canada) Since college, my sibling and I have played Santa for our parents. It’s our way of giving back. Yes, our parents still play Santa for us, and Santa gifts are, dare I say, now more anticipated than family gifts. – Eli (Seattle, Washington) Every year, we rent a big house or conference center for around 20 family members. We bring a Ping-Pong table if need be and we play card games, board games, puzzles, and, of course, Ping-Pong. Wednesday night is cheese streak night. On Thursday, we all work to make the Thanksgiving meal. Friday we hike and play, play, play. It never gets old. This year we are trying a new location, the Jersey Shore. – Joyce (Ottsville, Pennsylvania) My grandmother’s favorite color was purple; she passed about 20 years ago. Each year for Christmas, my mom and I wrap a special package in purple paper to give to each other from my grandmom, Mabelle. – Kimberleigh (Maryland) RELATED: We Asked Readers to Share the Best Compliments They’ve Received

items.descriptionOriginal: Every Tuesday, Toronto chef Maddy Goldberg ties on an apron at her local food bank and transforms whatever random ingredients she finds -- onions, carrots, a forgotten bag of raw red lentils -- into 100 hot meals for families who need them. The work traces back to a quiet moment of reckoning during her years in the fine dining industry, when she finally asked herself a question more people might benefit from sitting with: "What can I actually do?" For Goldberg, the answer wasn't grand -- it was a free Tuesday and a phone call to a food bank. "I wanted to do something where the goal wasn't to make money off of it," she says. "It was just to feed people, which is why I wanted to cook in the first place." Her story is a small reminder that the gap between caring about something and actually doing something about it is often narrower than it appears.

items.descriptionOriginal: In 1973, American brothers Michael and Brian McCormack mailed 1,360 letters in seven languages to government leaders across the globe, encouraging them to participate in the inaugural World Hello Day. “We wanted to do something to celebrate the importance of personal communication to preserving peace,” Michael, a senior at Harvard at the time, previously told the university paper, The Crimson . He and Brian had pooled their money to pay for the postage, with the goal of getting their recipients to agree to, quite literally, spread the word. The idea behind the holiday, observed every Nov. 21, is that differences should be addressed through peaceful conversation rather than conflict. To participate, all you have to do is say “hello” to 10 people. Fifteen countries pledged their support the first year; today, individuals in 180 have joined in — including 31 Nobel Peace Prize winners who sent the brothers letters championing World Hello Day. “It’s something people can do on their own in widely different places,” Michael explained to the Associated Press back in 1991. “It gives people a chance to do something about the world; it empowers them.” Ready to get started? Before you do, consider broadening your reach by learning how to say hello in a few different languages — below are 25 translations (plus two bonus ones, just for fun). Portuguese – olá Hindi – namaste Dutch – hallo Filipino – kumusta Ukrainian – pryvit Arabic – marhaban Polish – witam Greek – geiá sou Hebrew – shalom Mandarin – nǐ hǎo Spanish – hola Esperanto – saluton Yoruba – pẹlẹ o Hawaiian – aloha Japanese – kon’nichiwa Icelandic – halló Swahili – habari French – bonjour Zulu – sawubona Korean – annyeonghaseyo Persian – salām Turkish – merhaba Swedish – hej Samoan – talofa Italian – ciao Klingon (from Star Trek ) – nuqneH Dothraki (from Game of Thrones ) – m’athchomaroon

items.titleOriginal: Podcast Transcript November 20th, 2026— A Tourette’s wristband, a trash map and why you dread your plans
items.description: Περιγραφή επεισοδίου: Ένα βραχιολάκι που αναπτύχθηκε στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Νότιγχαμ στέλνει μικρούς ηλεκτρικούς παλμούς σε ένα νεύρο στον καρπό σας και για ορισμένα άτομα με Tourette, τα τικ τους εγκαθίστανται μέσα σε λίγα λεπτά από την ενεργοποίησή του. Μια 15χρονη χαρακτήρισε την πρώτη φορά που το δοκίμασε την καλύτερη μέρα της ζωής της. Η Arielle και η Karissa μπαίνουν επίσης σε ένα ελληνικό πλοίο που…
items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A wristband developed at the University of Nottingham sends small electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, their tics settle within moments of switching it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. Arielle and Karissa also get into a Greek ship that turned seven years of beach trash into a pollution map, a cancer therapy helping people with Céline Dion’s rare condition walk again, and the real reason you want to cancel plans you were excited to make. Learn more about April Surac and NeuraSensa: https://www.instagram.com/neurasensa/ If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Welcome and catch-up Arielle: Hi, I’m Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome to The Optimist Daily’s Weekly Roundup. How are you doing, Karissa? Karissa: I’m doing well over here. I’m feeling grateful and grounded as we head into the Thanksgiving week next week here in the US. Arielle: Do you have any fun Thanksgiving plans? Karissa: Um, I have multiple Thanksgivings actually I’ll be attending. So this weekend will be my Thanksgiving with my immediate family because everyone is kind of doing different things on actual Thanksgiving Day. And then I’ll be spending actual Thanksgiving with my partner’s family, so multiple celebrations going on this week. Arielle: Aw, that’s cute. And speaking of Thanksgiving, we are actually going to be missing next week’s full episode. We will have just a short greeting from our Optimist Daily family to yours. You can keep an eye out for that, or an ear out for that earlier in the week. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. Well, before we head into anything else, Arielle, how is everything with you? Arielle: Things are good. I was telling you before we hit record that my personal trainer was here today, and it was- excruciating. But yeah, it’s, it’s nice to be working on my strength. I think the benefit of working at The Optimist Daily is that you are exposed to so many solutions just for lifestyle changes that are going to help you live a healthier life and a longer life hopefully. And so yeah, even though the workouts are, uh, brutal sometimes- there’s always light at the end of the tunnel, and I know that it’s for my long-term health, and that kind of motivates me throughout the whole thing. Stay connected and support our work Karissa: There’s just so many great solutions on The Optimist Daily that we get the benefit of learning from. If you want these solutions to your inbox every day, we have a free daily newsletter, and we also have a weekly edition as well. The link to sign up for that is in the show notes. Arielle: We are also on all social media platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. There you can get more bite-sized versions of full solutions. As always, we welcome any comments, questions, or feedback. You can engage with us on those social platforms. You can slide into our DMs, or you can email me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. Karissa: We love to hear from you, and we also love when you share all these solutions in any format, whether you’re forwarding the newsletter, sharing this podcast, and leaving a good review, or reposting to your followers. Arielle: And it’s a wonderful and free way to support our mission. We are so, so grateful for The Optimist Daily community. You guys make this work so special and so meaningful. We appreciate every single like, follow, share, but we also have huge love for our Emissaries, people who financially donate to The Optimist Daily, whether that’s a one-time thing or a regular monthly or annual donation. Emissaries help us continue our mission, pushing it forward. Without them, we wouldn’t be able to do this amazing work. If you wanted to become an Emissary, now is a great time to do that, because we set a goal to get 100 new Emissaries by the end of this year. And I think we’ve maybe surpassed the halfway point at this moment in time? Karissa: We’re just about halfway there, yeah, to our Emissary goal. So help us cross that finish line by the end of the year so we can start off 2027 on an optimistic note, and just get these solutions to as many people as possible. This week’s solutions Arielle: Well, with all of that said, shall I jump into the solutions of the week? Karissa: Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news. “8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning” Arielle: The first solution we have is a lifestyle solution, something that all of us can apply to our lives right now to make it better, and the title is “8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning.” So this is especially for those of us who have a lot of flexibility regarding our schedule, for our remote workers and the like. But do you know when it’s 2:00 PM and you, you can’t really say where the morning went? Two time management experts say the fix for this doesn’t start when your alarm goes off. It actually starts the night before, and it’s way less intense than the really popular two-hour routines that are all over social media that, like, incorporate a bunch of, I don’t know, early morning journaling, and a stretching routine, and an ice plunge, and whatever the latest wellness trends are. Yeah. It can be a lot more simple. I think a lot of us will not be surprised that the number one morning habit, according to Julie Morgenstern, is about your phone. No screens for the first hour after you wake up and the last hour before bed. She compares managing phone time to managing sugar, and I have to say, I am not good at this. Karissa: Yeah. I, I am not good at managing sugar or screen time, so that’s a good comparison. Arielle: Yeah. I, uh… It’s so tempting, especially with the alarm on my phone. I swipe to turn the alarm off, and suddenly I’m already looking at the screen. So I think an analog old-school alarm clock might be a pretty good fix for this. Another habit that she says starts the morning off on the right foot is to begin the workday with the hardest, most important task. So even if the rest of the day falls apart, you’ve done the thing that matters most, that has the most impact. These are all really kind of simple things that you can do or keep in mind when you’re going through your morning. Karissa, what’s the first thing you do when you wake up? Karissa: Well, I mean, I do look at my phone first thing because I’m also swiping to turn off my alarm. So in turn, I’m also looking at all those notifications for a second before I get out of bed, and then I do have my little morning routine. I’ll get up, wash my face, brush my teeth, feed my cat, and put on a pot of coffee, and get some breakfast going. What about you? Arielle: After I have that quick minute on my phone, I also set the kettle to make my tea, and while that’s boiling, I’ll brush my teeth and usually do a little tidy up of the house because this is also my office, so I can’t focus if it’s kind of messy. Luckily, my dog makes me go out. So I do have, like, 20 to 30 minutes of just being out in nature and getting as much sunlight as I can, and I think that counts as one of these microbursts of self-care, which is defined as 5 to 20 minutes of doing something that recharges you. According to this article, the ideal morning routine has three or four elements max. Anything more and you’re setting yourself up for feeling guilty for missing something on a certain morning, or if you have, like, a long checklist of things to do, then it can put a lot of pressure on you as well. Um, so yeah, I did also like that aspect of the article that really emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be complicated. We’re not going through all of the tips here, like what to do the night before, but I highly recommend you check out the article for some more morning routine inspo. Karissa: Yeah, 100%. “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial” Arielle: All right. The next solution is titled “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial.” There’s a wristband out of the University of Nottingham that sends tiny electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, it calms their tics the moment they switch it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. I actually have a cousin who has Tourette’s. And his tics are not so… They’re, they… Like, he can go through the world and navigate it fine, but you can tell that he’s putting a lot of energy towards suppressing a lot as well. Yeah. I can only imagine how life-changing a device like this is that’s kind of subtle and elegant and simple and has a really big impact on just the mental and physical space that suppressing tics has, and also just having to go through the world with people staring at you, not really understanding what’s going on. The source for this article came from the BBC, and I actually took a minute to watch their video on this, and I highly recommend watching the video so that you can kind of get a better sense for how much impact this small device has on people. Karissa: Yeah. And how exactly does it work? Arielle: So how it works is kind of wild. There’s rhythmic pulses to the median nerve cha- which changes activity in the parts of the brain that control movement. In a trial of 121 people, tics dropped by about 25% on average, and it even works for people who don’t have Tourette’s. There was another teenager named Ollie, and he has a functional neurological disorder which makes his neck move constantly without him having any control over it. And when he tried the device, it also just completely stopped the neck movements. There’s a lot of potential for this wearable neurotech to positively affect the lives of people with Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety or even OCD. “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms” Arielle: The next solution is titled “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms.” Okay, so we’ve already talked about the midterms, but we haven’t talked about this specific area of it. I think most people have never eaten foie gras in their lives, and yet it produced some of the most lopsided votes of election night. Animals came out of these midterms surprisingly well, and there’s a pattern in what passed and what didn’t that I found quite interesting. First of all, do you know how foie gras is made? Have you ever eaten it, Karissa? Karissa: Never eaten it, and I didn’t really know much about it until this article actually. Arielle: Yeah. I, I wanna say I have never tried it, but I can’t be for certain. I, I- worked a lot in the hospitality industry and, uh, tried a lot of different things, but it makes me feel a bit bad if I, if I had, because they basically, like, force feed ducks. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Um, or is it geese? But they- I think it’s geese, yeah … force feed them, and it produces this pâté-like, um I’m not describing this well, but people who know foie gras, you know what I’m talking about. Yeah. And those of you who don’t, look it up ’cause it is a l- well, it’s kinda disturbing. Um, so DC voted 73% and Denver 66% to ban foie gras sales, and a DC chef has been hosting foie gras tasting dinners to fund a lawsuit against the ban. So, yeah. Oh. There’s a, a little bit of tension there. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Colorado rejected a constitutional right to hunt and fish, and the fight came down to two words: traditional methods, which critics said could have brought back leg-hold traps and poison as, um, as hunting strategies. Denver voters said no to banning fur and slaughterhouses in 2024, but yes to banning foie gras now. So it seems like narrow bans on one practice seem to have a much easier time going through than ones that take on a whole industry for, of course, concerns about employment and yeah, having to restructure or get rid of a whole industry. Um- so more people are actually paying attention to how their food is produced, even when they’re not really changing their diet. Like, they’re not going vegan, they’re not going vegetarian, but they are concerned about how their food is produced and where it comes from. “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map” Arielle: The next solution is titled “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map.” The team that’s doing the cleanup isn’t just picking up trash. They’re noting down every single piece of it. This project consists of one ship, 20 people, five inflatable boats, and 1,140 tons of trash pulled off remote shores since 2019. For a visual, that’s 22 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of pollution. They’ve built what they say is the largest marine pollution database in the Mediterranean, and university researchers are using it to map plastic on the seabed. The data led them somewhere they didn’t necessarily expect. A lot of the trash came from inland, from rivers and illegal dumps, so they also started a second program on land. Beach cleanups are pretty popular, but there’s growing frustration that cleaning up the beach doesn’t necessarily stop the flow, or it doesn’t nip the issue in the bud. But it’s nice to see that citizen science and cleanup data are increasingly shaping policy on plastics. “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it” Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with you before I hand it over to Karissa is a Local Changemaker. This one’s titled “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it.” This week’s Local Changemaker is April Surac, a Florida teenager who grew up in her family’s furniture workshop and has a younger sister who has autism. Her installations are made of fabric with sensors built in, so the surfaces shift under your hand and the light and sound change as you move through the room. They’re designed for people with autism and people with sensory or cognitive differences, including dementia. More than 15,000 people have experienced the installations, and she sent over 250 sensory kits to families, schools, and hospitals. And she funds a lot of it with her own savings. I think she started this when she was only 16 or 17, which is so impressive. She’s also a 2025 Barron Prize winner, and she’s now working on gallery commissions in New York, LA, and London. Plus, she is developing a wearable sensory tool, and she’s moving towards patents for that. I think it’s really encouraging that a lot of people are growing in their awareness and compassion for diverse bodies and experiences. Sensory-friendly hours are popping up at museums, grocery stores, and movie theaters, which comes from people just realizing how much public spaces assume about our bodies. It’s wonderful to see the shift from accessibility compliance to designing for everyone from the very beginning of a project. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. And I really loved that she had a line that said, “Design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” And that’s something we don’t see enough of in our world. So I think this is just such a fascinating, uh, story, what she’s doing, and I feel so honored to be able to share her story here on The Optimist Daily as one of our local changemakers this year. “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade” Karissa: “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade.” So homelessness in the US dropped more than 6% last year. That’s about 49,000 fewer people without housing, and the biggest one-year drop in over a decade. One of the biggest points here in this article is that veteran homelessness is down nearly 60% since 2010, and advocates say it’s proof that putting people in housing first with no strings attached actually works. On the other hand, the Trump administration credits immigration enforcement and encampment crackdowns to this decline, but advocates say their data shows cities with camping bans did worse than average. It’s important to note, too, that not everyone saw a drop because people who’ve been homeless for a long time increased slightly, and that’s the group that both sides are fighting over the best way to help them. But yeah, I mean, in a time where housing affordability is one of the biggest issues in the country right now, this is encouraging news nonetheless. “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling” Karissa: The next solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling.” So you know when you’re the one who made the plans, and then an hour before you’re supposed to leave, you’re on the couch drafting a text reading, “I’m so sorry, something came up,” or, “I feel sick.” There’s actually a name for this experience, and there’s a surprisingly simple trick for getting out the door anyway. Arielle, have you had this feeling before? Arielle: Oh my gosh, this is so relatable. I do find myself kind of dreading plans, and I try not to cancel. I try to push myself through it, but there are some days where I’m just like, “Ooh, I don’t wanna hop on my bike and go through the rain,” and- you know, I don’t wanna see anyone. I don’t wanna talk to anyone. I’m so tired. So yeah, this solution definitely spoke to me. Karissa: And I’m sure probably all of us have been there at some point or another. But this feeling is called anticipatory anxiety. 55% of Gen Z say they feel relief when plans get canceled, and a UK survey found that 68% of under 34s have flaked. But there’s a simple therapist-approved trick to get over this anxiety. Set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, shower and get dressed without debating it. So kind of just going forward with it without overthinking it. I think flaking has become so normal now that some people kind of dread planning anything, including their own birthdays and events. And in a time where loneliness is being talked about as a public health issue, canceling plans is a small part of this bigger picture. I feel like it’s kind of a lot easier to cancel plans, too, especially ’cause you don’t even have to call someone to cancel. You just send a text. But usually it’s better for all of us to push through and go forward with that connection anyways. Arielle: I like how this article said that part of the strategy is to imagine a moment when you did push through and you did go to whatever event or whatever gathering or, or meetup that you were once dreading. And chances are you ended up enjoying yourself, and you forgot all about that dread that you had before you actually stepped out the door. And there’s a lot of discussion around protecting our own peace, which I think is valid, but it can make it a lot easier to cop out. We have to be really careful about whether or not we are protecting our peace and we do need that break, because sometimes we definitely do need to take a moment for ourselves, or if we’re just letting the anxiety take over. “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers” Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers.” Two of the most toxic forever chemicals have dropped by almost a third in England’s rivers over the last 10 years, and in fish by about half. The UK basically banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and the river data now shows the effect, that 30% and 29% drops. But the catch is the chemicals didn’t actually disappear. The total amount is probably the same, but it’s just been diluted and washed out to sea. So it’s still out there, but there’s not as much, you know, going in. There are about 15,000 types of PFAS, and England has just two facilities that can destroy them for good, so not a lot, uh, out there that can get them out of here. PFAS are in the news constantly. They’re in our drinking water, in non-stick pans, rain jackets, and people are increasingly worried about them in their own homes, with good reason of course, because they don’t go away. And the UK government just announced it will start measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies, so we should have more data on, you know, how exactly forever these chemicals are, and hopefully that will inform more policy in the future. “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again” Karissa: The next solution is “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again.” Stiff person syndrome is a rare condition that Céline Dion lives with, and until now, there’s been no real treatment for it. Doctors at the Mayo Clinic tried a therapy that’s normally used for cancer, and some patients who needed help walking are now miraculously back at work. CAR-T therapy is something that takes your own immune cells, reprograms them in a lab, and puts them back to wipe out the cells causing the disease. Patients in this one got a single treatment, and one patient, Jonathan, went from needing his family’s help with basic tasks to returning to his favorite hobbies like hunting and fishing again, and he says he hasn’t had a single episode since. This condition, like I mentioned at the beginning, was, you know, kind of brought into the spotlight by Céline Dion’s diagnosis in 2022. She was part of a documentary that brought this condition to the fore. So yeah, CAR-T therapies are one of the biggest stories in medicine right now, and researchers are also trying it out on lupus, MS, and other autoimmune diseases. But as of now, these therapies are incredibly expensive, so it raises the questions about who will have access to them. But hopefully with all medical breakthroughs and advancements, it will become more accessible to more people who need it. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them)” Karissa: The last solution I have to share is also a lifestyle-oriented one, and has to do kind of with Thanksgiving and the holidays coming up. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them).” So yeah, this holiday party season is about to start, and this one’s all about the stuff your guests notice but would never mention. This goes over a lot of great, uh, you know, pointers about hosting. One prominent one is the parking and coats problem. A party can be beautifully decorated and still feel chaotic if peoples have to circle the block searching for parking, or if they have to hold their jackets for 30 minutes without somewhere to put them. Arielle: The tip that spoke to me was about letting yourself as a host enjoy the gathering as well, instead of always being concerned with, like, cleaning up or prepping things or grabbing whatever, because the people who are there, the people you invited, are there to presumably spend time with you and each other. And it can put people on edge if you’re just constantly, like, fluttering around and, you know, making sure that everything is running perfectly without actually taking the time to settle in. And that, that is kind of challenging for me. Um, especially because I enjoy cleaning. But that’s definitely something that I’m going to be taking to heart this holiday season. And yeah, there’s a lot of other really great tips here as well. But yeah, exciting to get into the festive spirit. Karissa: That’s all the solutions we had this week on The Optimist Daily. Closing quote Arielle: Before we wrap up this episode, we have an inspiring quote, as usual. Karissa: Yes. The quote is, “My turn shall also come: I sense the spreading of a wing.” And that’s from Osip Mandelstam. Very poetic. Yeah, a poetic end to this edition of the weekly roundup. Thanksgiving sign-off Arielle: Yes. We will be back… Oh, we won’t actually be back next week with a full episode, but we will have a special Thanksgiving greeting from The Optimist Daily team to all of you. But in the meantime, Karissa and I wish you all a very, very happy, restful weekend. items.descriptionOriginal: If you’re sitting down for seafood, should you order the farmed or wild-caught fish? In this day of over-exploited seas, the farmed fillet might seem like a better choice. And yet, in many cases, those farmed salmon or trout also contribute to over-fishing , because they’re raised on diets of wild-caught sardines, herring, anchovies, or mackerel . But researchers have now developed a potential solution to this problem: a meat-free, algal diet that farmed fish can thrive on. As human populations expand, farmed fish are becoming an increasing protein source. Roughly 100 million tons of farmed fish and crustaceans are harvested worldwide each year. In order to feed them, at least 20 millions of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil each year—most of it consumed by farmed predatory species such as salmon and trout. But even non-predatory farmed fish like tilapia have hidden costs, because they’re often raised on cornmeal or soy, requiring agricultural land that might otherwise feed humans directly. A team of researchers at the University of California Santa Cruz has spent years developing fish feeds based on two types of marine algae, called Nannochloropsis and Schizochytrium , which are also being used or studied as sources for biofuels, farm animal feed , and nutritional additives for human foods. In 2020, the team showed that farmed tilapia grew normally on blends of these two algae . items.title: Cafe Server Επιστρέφει Τσάντα 20.000 $ που άφησε πίσω το ζευγάρι
items.titleOriginal: Cafe Server Returns Bag of $20,000 Left Behind by Couple
items.description: Στο αποκορύφωμα ενός σαββατιάτικου δείπνου στη Σιγκαπούρη, ένας σερβιτόρος καφέ ονόματι Lau Guat Toh εντόπισε μια τσάντα χωρίς επίβλεψη και έκανε ό,τι της ήρθε φυσικά - την προστάτεψε, την έβαλε κάτω από μια κάμερα ασφαλείας και περίμενε. Μέσα ήταν 20.000 δολάρια σε μετρητά, αρκετά για να κροταλίσουν τους περισσότερους, αλλά η Λάου και οι συνάδελφοί της «δεν τόλμησαν να το αγγίξουν», μια λεπτομέρεια που λέει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At the height of a Saturday dinner rush in Singapore, a coffee shop server named Lau Guat Toh spotted an unattended bag and did what came naturally to her - she protected it, placed it under a security camera, and waited. Inside was $20,000 in cash, enough to rattle most people, but Lau and her colleagues "did not dare touch" it, a detail that says more about their character than any declaration of honesty could. The bag's owner, a noodle manufacturer who had rushed off to a friend's wake, returned at 11pm simply trying his luck, and found everything intact. What lingers in the story is the quiet ecosystem of goodness surrounding the moment: a boss who had spent his evening delivering donated soup to elderly residents, a customer whose first response to losing a fortune was not panic but acceptance, and a server who plans to keep her $200 reward as a souvenir rather than spend it. "If something is meant to come, it will come," said the man who lost the money - and somehow, in this small coffee shop in Bedok, it did.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage.
